sections.h: What happens when a ConfigMap changes
sections.body:
Most people get this wrong the first time. Changing a ConfigMap never restarts anything, and what a running Pod sees depends on how it reads the value:
- Environment variables are set once, when the container starts. They never change while it runs.
- Mounted files are updated in place. The kubelet notices the change on its next sync and swaps the files, usually within a minute or so.
- A file mounted with `subPath` (one file into an existing folder) is never updated.
- Even an updated file only helps if your app reads it again. Most apps read config once at start.

So for hello-devops, which uses env vars, a new greeting needs new Pods. The tool for that is `kubectl rollout restart deployment/hello-devops`. It writes the current time into an annotation in the Pod template. The template changed, so the Deployment does a normal rolling update, and every new Pod starts with the new values.

There is a neater trick that tools use. Put something that changes with the config into the Pod template:
- Kustomize's `configMapGenerator` adds a hash of the content to the ConfigMap's name, such as `hello-config-7g2m9dfk8t`. New content means a new name and a new template, so a rollout happens by itself.
- Helm charts often put a checksum of the config into a template annotation, with the same effect.

Day 37 covers both tools.

refs.title: ConfigMaps: mounted ConfigMaps are updated automatically

sections.body:
Editing a ConfigMap in place has a hidden cost. A Deployment rollback brings back the old Pod template, but not the old ConfigMap. If you changed both and then roll back, the old code runs with the new settings.

The fix is to treat config like images: never change a version, make a new one.
1. Create `hello-config-v2` next to `hello-config-v1`.
2. Point the Deployment's `envFrom` at `hello-config-v2`. That is a template change, so a rollout starts.
3. To roll back, `kubectl rollout undo` brings back the template that points at `v1`, and `v1` still exists.

Kubernetes helps you keep that promise with `immutable: true`. Once set, nobody can change the data, and it cannot be switched off again. You can only delete the object and create a new one. Immutable ConfigMaps and Secrets also save work for the API server, because kubelets stop watching them for changes. That matters in clusters with thousands of them.

This is exactly what Kustomize's hash suffix does for you: every content change is a new, versioned name. For the lab, one plain ConfigMap and `rollout restart` are enough. Know the pattern for when config changes start causing incidents.

sections.h: Secrets, and why base64 is not encryption
sections.body:
A **Secret** looks like a ConfigMap, but it is meant for sensitive values: passwords, API tokens, TLS keys. Pods use it the same three ways: `env` with `secretKeyRef`, `envFrom` with `secretRef`, or a volume.

Its values sit in `data`, encoded in base64. Base64 is a way to write any bytes as plain letters, so binary keys fit in YAML. It is not encryption. Anyone can reverse it with one command, as the worked example shows. You can also write plain text in a `stringData` field, and the API server encodes it for you.

Secrets have a `type` that tells tools what keys to expect:
- `Opaque`: anything you like. The default.
- `kubernetes.io/dockerconfigjson`: login details for a private registry such as GHCR, used through `imagePullSecrets`.
- `kubernetes.io/tls`: a certificate and its private key, used by Gateways (Day 36).
- `kubernetes.io/basic-auth` and `kubernetes.io/ssh-auth`: a user and password, or an SSH key.

So what is different about a Secret? A few real things:
- Kubernetes sends a Secret only to nodes that run a Pod that needs it.
- On the node, the kubelet keeps mounted Secrets in memory (tmpfs), never on disk.
- `kubectl describe` shows the size of each value, not the value.
- Access rules (RBAC) can allow reading ConfigMaps but not Secrets.

By default, though, Secrets are stored unencrypted in etcd. And anyone who can create a Pod in a namespace can mount, and so read, every Secret in it.

The Kubernetes docs list the steps that actually protect Secrets. Here they are, plus one that people often forget (number 3):
1. Turn on encryption at rest. The API server then encrypts Secrets before writing them to etcd, so a stolen backup or disk shows nothing.
2. Limit who can read Secrets with RBAC (role-based access control, Day 38). Very few people and programs need `get` or `list` on Secrets.
3. Limit who can create Pods in namespaces that hold important Secrets, because a Pod can mount any Secret in its namespace.
4. Give each container only the Secrets it needs.

On a cluster you run yourself, encryption at rest means an `EncryptionConfiguration` file for the API server. The best setups use a KMS provider, where a cloud key service holds the real key. Managed clusters such as EKS, AKS and GKE offer this with their own key services, and some turn it on by default. Check your provider's docs.

How the app reads a Secret matters too. Many teams prefer mounted files to env vars. Env vars are easy to leak: a crash report, a debug page or a `printenv` in a support session can print them all. A file is read only when the code asks for it.

None of this changes one rule. A Secret manifest with real values must never go into git, not even in a private repo. Base64 in git is plain text that stays in the history forever.

If Secrets cannot live in git, where do they come from when you deploy from git? Teams pick one of a few patterns:
- External Secrets Operator: the real value lives in a vault, such as AWS Secrets Manager, Google Secret Manager or HashiCorp Vault. You commit an `ExternalSecret` object that says which value to fetch. A controller in the cluster fetches it and writes a normal Secret, and refreshes it when the vault changes.
- Sealed Secrets: you encrypt a Secret with the cluster's public key, using the `kubeseal` tool, and commit the resulting `SealedSecret`. Only the controller in the cluster holds the private key, so only it can decrypt.
- SOPS: you encrypt the values inside YAML files with a cloud key or an age key. The files go into git, and your deploy tool decrypts them on the way in.
- The Secrets Store CSI Driver: the vault's values are mounted straight into the Pod as files, often without creating a Kubernetes Secret at all.

Which one? If your company already has a vault, External Secrets Operator is the common choice, because the vault stays the single place to rotate a password. For a small team without one, Sealed Secrets is the simplest to start with.

hello-devops has no real secrets yet, so the lab has no Secret file. Day 40 shows how these tools fit into GitOps, and Day 53 goes deeper into secrets and access.

lessons.analogy: A ConfigMap read as env vars is like a note in a new employee's locker on their first day. They read it once and never look again, so a changed note only reaches the next new hire. A mounted file is the notice board in the hallway, which people see whenever they walk past. A Secret is the same note in an envelope marked confidential, but the envelope is not sealed, which is why base64 hides nothing. The comparison breaks on reach. Anyone who can create Pods in a namespace can read all its Secrets, as if anyone allowed to hire staff could open every envelope the team holds.

worked.title: Watch a ConfigMap change reach a Pod, or not

steps.say: Apply the demo from the examples folder in the scratch namespace (create it again with `kubectl create namespace scratch` if you deleted it). It creates a ConfigMap with `COLOR: blue` and a Pod that prints the value as an env var and as a file every 5 seconds.
steps.code:
$ kubectl apply -n scratch -f k8s/examples/config-demo.yaml
configmap/demo-config created
pod/config-demo created
$ kubectl logs -n scratch config-demo
env=blue file=blue
env=blue file=blue

steps.say: Change the value in the ConfigMap, then follow the logs. For a while nothing changes. After the kubelet's next sync, the file shows the new value. The env var never does.
steps.code:
$ kubectl patch configmap demo-config -n scratch --type merge -p '{"data":{"COLOR":"green"}}'
configmap/demo-config patched
$ kubectl logs -n scratch config-demo -f --tail=3
env=blue file=blue
env=blue file=blue
env=blue file=green
env=blue file=green
^C

steps.say: See how the kubelet swaps the file safely. The real data sits in a timestamped folder, and `..data` is a link to it. On a change, the kubelet writes a new folder and moves the link in one step, so the app never reads half a file. This link trick is also why `subPath` mounts never update.
steps.code:
$ kubectl exec -n scratch config-demo -- ls -la /config
total 12
drwxrwxrwx    3 root     root          4096 Oct 30 09:41 .
drwxr-xr-x    1 root     root          4096 Oct 30 09:38 ..
drwxr-xr-x    2 root     root          4096 Oct 30 09:41 ..2026_10_30_09_41_07.2716545396
lrwxrwxrwx    1 root     root            32 Oct 30 09:41 ..data -> ..2026_10_30_09_41_07.2716545396
lrwxrwxrwx    1 root     root            12 Oct 30 09:38 COLOR -> ..data/COLOR

steps.say: A bare Pod has no `rollout restart`, so replace it: `replace --force` deletes the Pod and creates it again from the same spec. The new container starts with the new env var.
steps.code:
$ kubectl get pod config-demo -n scratch -o yaml | kubectl replace --force -f -
pod "config-demo" deleted from scratch namespace
pod/config-demo replaced
$ kubectl logs -n scratch config-demo
env=green file=green

steps.say: Now a Secret. Create one from a literal value, read the stored field, then decode it. Base64 kept the value out of sight for exactly one command.
steps.code:
$ kubectl create secret generic demo-secret -n scratch --from-literal=password='s3cr3t!'
secret/demo-secret created
$ kubectl get secret demo-secret -n scratch -o jsonpath='{.data.password}'
czNjcjN0IQ==
$ kubectl get secret demo-secret -n scratch -o jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 --decode
s3cr3t!

steps.say: Delete the scratch namespace. Everything in it goes: the demo ConfigMap, the Pod and the Secret.
steps.code:
$ kubectl delete namespace scratch
namespace "scratch" deleted

code.title: k8s/configmap.yaml
code.src:
# Settings for the app (Day 34). Each key becomes an environment variable (see envFrom in deployment.yaml).
# Env vars are read once at start: after you change a value, run
#   kubectl rollout restart deployment/hello-devops -n hello
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: hello-config
  namespace: hello
data:
  GREETING: "Hello from Kubernetes!"
  REDIS_HOST: "redis" # the name of the Redis Service in this namespace

code.title: k8s/redis.yaml
code.src:
# Redis keeps the visit counter, shared by all app pods (Day 34).
# No disk here: the count resets if the Redis pod restarts (Day 36 covers storage).
# Day 35 explains the readiness probe and the resources below.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: redis
  namespace: hello
  labels:
    app: redis
spec:
  replicas: 1
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: redis
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: redis
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: redis
          image: redis:8-alpine
          ports:
            - containerPort: 6379
          readinessProbe:
            exec:
              command: ["redis-cli", "ping"]
            periodSeconds: 5
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 50m
              memory: 64Mi
            limits:
              memory: 128Mi
---
# A ClusterIP Service: reachable only inside the cluster, as "redis" from namespace hello.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: redis
  namespace: hello
  labels:
    app: redis
spec:
  selector:
    app: redis
  ports:
    - name: redis
      port: 6379
      targetPort: 6379

code.title: k8s/deployment.yaml (Day 34 version; Day 35 adds probes and resources)
code.src:
# Runs 3 copies (pods) of hello-devops and replaces any that die.
# Day 34 version: adds envFrom. Day 35 adds probes and resources.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  namespace: hello
  labels:
    app: hello-devops
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello-devops # must match the pod labels below
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0 # never drop below 3 ready pods during an update
      maxSurge: 1 # add at most 1 extra pod at a time
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello-devops
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: hello-devops:1.0.0
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent # use the image kind loaded; do not pull it
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8000
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: hello-config # every key in the ConfigMap becomes an env var

# Day 34 version: adds the ConfigMap and Redis. Day 35 adds hpa.yaml.
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1

code.title: k8s/examples/config-demo.yaml
code.src:
# Day 34: watch one ConfigMap value reach a container twice: as an env var and as a file.
#   kubectl apply -n scratch -f k8s/examples/config-demo.yaml
#   kubectl logs -n scratch config-demo -f
#   kubectl patch configmap demo-config -n scratch --type merge -p '{"data":{"COLOR":"green"}}'
apiVersion: v1
kind: ConfigMap
metadata:
  name: demo-config
data:
  COLOR: "blue"
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: config-demo
spec:
  containers:
    - name: show
      image: busybox:1.37
      # Every 5 seconds, print the env var and the file side by side.
      command: ["sh", "-c", "while true; do echo \"env=$COLOR file=$(cat /config/COLOR)\"; sleep 5; done"]
      envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: demo-config # COLOR becomes an env var, set once when the container starts
      volumeMounts:
        - name: config
          mountPath: /config # COLOR also becomes the file /config/COLOR, which the kubelet keeps up to date
  volumes:
    - name: config
      configMap:
        name: demo-config

lessons.mistake: Committing a Secret manifest to git because "it is encoded". Base64 is not encryption, and git keeps every old version, so the value is public to anyone who can read the repo, forever. If it happens, rotate the password or token at once, then switch to External Secrets Operator, Sealed Secrets or SOPS so real values never reach git.
lessons.real_world: At PayLite, each service's non-secret settings live in a ConfigMap generated by Kustomize, so every config change rolls the Pods automatically and can be rolled back with the code. Database passwords live in AWS Secrets Manager. External Secrets Operator syncs them into the cluster every hour, and the clusters have KMS encryption at rest turned on.

steps: Write `k8s/configmap.yaml` and `k8s/redis.yaml`. Add `envFrom` to `k8s/deployment.yaml`, add both new files to `k8s/kustomization.yaml`, and run `kubectl apply -k k8s`.

Check what one container really has with `kubectl exec ... -- printenv GREETING`.
Change `GREETING` in `configmap.yaml` and apply again. Call curl. Which greeting do you get, and why?
Pick up the change with `kubectl rollout restart` and follow the rollout. Confirm that curl shows the new greeting.
Find what `rollout restart` changed in the Pod template: print the template's annotations with a jsonpath query.
Create a Secret named `hello-secret` in namespace `hello` with a key `API_TOKEN` and any fake value. Read it back with `-o yaml`, then decode it. Compare with what `kubectl describe secret` shows.
Write down who in a real cluster could read that token. Then delete the Secret and commit the four files (not the Secret).

Pods stuck in `CreateContainerConfigError`? The name in `envFrom` must match the ConfigMap's `metadata.name` exactly, in the same namespace.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences what happens to a running Deployment when you change its ConfigMap, and how you make the Pods use the new values. Mention env vars, mounted files and rollout restart.
explain_back.answer: Changing a ConfigMap does not restart any Pod. Containers that read it as environment variables keep the old values, because env vars are set only when a container starts. Containers that mount it as files see the new content after the kubelet's next sync, if the app reads the file again. To make every Pod use new env values, run `kubectl rollout restart`, which changes the Pod template and starts a normal rolling update. Tools like Kustomize get the same effect by giving each config version a new name.

recap: ConfigMaps hold plain settings outside the image; Pods read them as env vars, envFrom or files.
Env vars never change in a running container; mounted files update, except with subPath.
`kubectl rollout restart` or a new ConfigMap name in the template rolls Pods onto new config.
Immutable, versioned ConfigMaps make config changes safe to roll back with the code.
Secrets are base64-encoded, not encrypted; protect them with encryption at rest, RBAC and care about who can create Pods.
Keep real secret values out of git with External Secrets Operator, Sealed Secrets or SOPS.

check.q: An nginx Pod mounts `nginx.conf` from a ConfigMap as a whole folder. You change the ConfigMap. What happens?
options: nginx notices the change and restarts with the new config
The file changes soon, but nginx uses it only after a reload
Nothing changes until someone deletes and recreates the Pod
The Pod fails, because mounted ConfigMap files are read-only
check.why: Mounted files are updated in place, but a program that read its config at start must reload it (or be restarted) to use the new file.

check.q: A teammate says: "Our Secrets are safe, the YAML shows only base64." What is the best answer?
options: True, as long as the cluster runs Kubernetes 1.30 or newer
True, because kubectl hides Secret values from every user
False, because Secrets cannot hold binary data like keys
False: anyone can decode base64; encryption and access rules protect them
check.why: Base64 is an encoding anyone can reverse; real protection is encrypting etcd and limiting who can read Secrets or create Pods.

check.q: You change both the image and the ConfigMap data of a Deployment, then roll back with `kubectl rollout undo`. Which combination runs now?
options: Old image with the old ConfigMap data
New image with the old ConfigMap data
Old image with the new ConfigMap data
Nothing, because undo refuses to run
check.why: Undo restores the old Pod template, but a ConfigMap edited in place is not part of it, so the old code meets the new settings.

interview.q: What is the difference between a ConfigMap and a Secret?
interview.a: Both store key-value data that Pods consume as environment variables or files. ConfigMaps are for non-sensitive settings and are shown in plain text. Secrets are for sensitive data: values are base64-encoded, sent only to nodes that need them, kept in tmpfs on nodes and can be restricted separately with RBAC. They are not encrypted by default, so production clusters enable encryption at rest, often with a KMS provider.

interview.q: How do you make Pods pick up a changed ConfigMap?
interview.a: Env vars are fixed at container start, so the Pods must be recreated, usually with `kubectl rollout restart`, which changes a template annotation and triggers a rolling update. Mounted files update in place after the kubelet syncs, but the app has to reload them, and subPath mounts never update. A cleaner pattern is versioned or hash-suffixed ConfigMap names, as Kustomize's configMapGenerator does, so a config change is a template change and can be rolled back.

interview.q: How would you manage secrets for apps deployed with GitOps?
interview.a: Never commit plain Secret manifests, because base64 is readable and git history is permanent. With an existing vault, I would use External Secrets Operator: git holds an ExternalSecret reference, and the controller syncs the real value from AWS Secrets Manager or Vault. Without one, Sealed Secrets or SOPS let you commit encrypted values that only the cluster or the deploy tool can decrypt. On top of that: encryption at rest, tight RBAC on Secrets and on Pod creation, and rotation when anything leaks.

deeper.body:
How long does a mounted ConfigMap take to update? The docs give a formula rather than a number: the kubelet's sync period plus the delay of its cache. By default the kubelet watches ConfigMaps, so the cache delay is small, and the sync period is about a minute. In practice, plan for up to a minute or two, and never for "instantly".

Projected volumes let one folder hold data from several sources. A `projected` volume can combine keys from ConfigMaps, Secrets, the Downward API (facts about the Pod itself, such as its name and labels) and a short-lived ServiceAccount token. It all appears as files in one place, which is tidy for apps that expect a single config folder.

Secrets have a few more corners worth knowing:
- Environment variables from a Secret are visible to anything that can read the process environment. Inside the container that includes every child process. On the node, it includes anyone who can inspect the container.
- `kubectl get secret -o yaml` prints the values for anyone with `get` permission. The `describe` output hides them, but that is a convenience, not a control.
- A ServiceAccount used to get a long-lived token Secret automatically. Since Kubernetes 1.24 that no longer happens. Pods get short-lived tokens through a projected volume, and those expire and rotate on their own.

Encryption at rest works like this on a self-managed cluster. You give the API server an `EncryptionConfiguration` file that lists providers for the `secrets` resource:
- `identity` means no encryption, which is the default.
- `aescbc`, `aesgcm` and `secretbox` encrypt with a key kept in the same file on the control-plane node.
- `kms` (version 2) asks an outside key service to wrap the data keys, so the real key never sits on the node.

The first provider in the list encrypts new writes, and all listed providers can decrypt. Existing Secrets stay as they were until they are written again. So after you turn encryption on, you rewrite every Secret once, for example with `kubectl get secrets -A -o json | kubectl replace -f -`.

On kind you could try this by mounting a config file into the control-plane node with `extraMounts` and a kubeadm patch. It is a good weekend exercise, not something you need for this course.

Finally, a word on size and count. A Secret, like a ConfigMap, is limited to 1 MiB. If you find yourself storing large files in either, a volume or an object store is usually the better place.

lessons.title: Health checks, resources and scaling
lessons.goal: By the end you can give hello-devops health checks and resource settings that match what it needs, autoscale it with an HPA, and control where its Pods run and how many may be down at once.

guess.q: A container uses more CPU than its CPU limit for a few seconds. What does Kubernetes do?
options: Kills the container and starts a new one
Slows it down, and it keeps running
Moves the Pod to a node with more CPU
Marks the Pod not ready until it calms down
guess.why: CPU can be handed out in smaller slices, so the kernel throttles the container and it runs slower. Only going over the memory limit gets a container killed.

terms.plain: A regular check of a container; after enough failures in a row, the kubelet restarts it.
A regular check; while it fails, the Pod gets no traffic from Services, but keeps running.
A check that holds back the other probes until a slow app has finished starting.
The CPU and memory the scheduler reserves for a container on a node.
The most CPU or memory a container may use; over the memory limit it is killed.
Guaranteed, Burstable or BestEffort: decides which Pods a short node evicts first.
An object that changes a Deployment's number of Pods based on metrics such as CPU.
A rule that limits how many Pods of an app planned work, such as a node drain, may take down at once.

sections.h: Running is not the same as healthy
sections.body:
Since Day 31, Kubernetes has restarted your containers when their process exits. That covers crashes. It does not cover an app that is still running but stuck, or one that is up but cannot reach its database. From the outside, both look like a healthy process.

A **probe** is a small check that the kubelet runs against a container on a timer. The kubelet is the agent on each node (Day 30), so the check runs right next to the container. The lab uses HTTP probes: the kubelet sends a GET request, and any status from 200 to 399 counts as a pass. A probe can also run a command in the container (`exec`), open a TCP connection (`tcpSocket`) or call a gRPC health check.

There are three probes. Each asks a different question, and a failure leads to a different action:
- Startup probe: "Have you finished starting?" Until it passes, the other two wait. If it never passes, the container is restarted.
- Liveness probe: "Are you stuck?" After enough failures in a row, the kubelet kills the container and starts a new one.
- Readiness probe: "Can you take traffic right now?" While it fails, the Pod leaves the Service's endpoints. Nothing restarts.

hello-devops has two endpoints made for this. The `/healthz` endpoint answers as long as the Python process can serve a request. The `/readyz` endpoint also pings Redis and returns 503 when Redis is down. Today you add all three probes to `k8s/deployment.yaml`: startup and liveness on `/healthz`, readiness on `/readyz`. Redis already has one: `k8s/redis.yaml` from Day 34 runs `redis-cli ping` as an `exec` readiness probe.

One surprise: Kubernetes does not run the `HEALTHCHECK` line from your Dockerfile (Part 3). That line only matters when you run the image with plain Docker. In a cluster, probes take its place.

refs.title: Configure liveness, readiness and startup probes
Kubernetes health probes explained (Tech Tutorials with Piyush, CKA series)

sections.h: Probe timing, and the liveness trap
sections.body:
Every probe has the same four timing settings, and you should be able to read them:
- `periodSeconds`: how often to check. Default 10.
- `timeoutSeconds`: how long one check may take. Default 1.
- `failureThreshold`: how many failures in a row before the kubelet acts. Default 3.
- `initialDelaySeconds`: how long to wait after the container starts. Default 0.

Multiply them to see how fast each probe acts. In the lab's Deployment, the startup probe allows 30 failures, 2 seconds apart, so the app gets up to 60 seconds to boot. The liveness probe needs 3 misses 10 seconds apart, so a stuck container is replaced after about 30 seconds. The readiness probe checks every 5 seconds and acts after 2 misses, so a Pod leaves the Service within about 10 seconds.

Now the trap, which catches many teams. Never make the liveness probe depend on something outside the container, such as a database. Picture Redis going down for a minute while `/healthz` checks Redis. Every hello-devops Pod fails liveness at about the same time, and the kubelet restarts all of them. The restarts cannot fix Redis, and while they happen no Pod can serve anything. The [probes docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/workloads/pods/probes/) warn that a wrong liveness probe "can lead to cascading failures".

Readiness is the right place for dependency checks, because failing it only pauses traffic. Even there, be careful. If every Pod fails readiness at once, the Service has no endpoints left and users get errors. That is why the lab's readiness probe allows a 2-second timeout and 2 failures instead of the tightest values.

Readiness also guards rollouts. On Day 32 a rolling update waited for new Pods to become ready before it removed old ones. That wait is this probe.

sections.h: Requests and limits: what you reserve and what you may use
sections.body:
Each container can say how much CPU and memory it needs. CPU is counted in cores: `100m` means 100 millicores, a tenth of one core. Memory is counted in bytes: `128Mi` means 128 mebibytes.

There are two numbers, and they do different jobs:
- A request is what the scheduler reserves. It puts a Pod only on a node whose unreserved room fits the request. If no node fits, the Pod stays `Pending`.
- A limit is the most the container may use. The Linux kernel enforces it while the container runs, with cgroups (the kernel feature Docker also uses to limit containers).

What happens at the limit depends on the resource, and this trips most people up. CPU time can be handed out in smaller slices, so a container at its CPU limit is throttled: it keeps running, only slower. Memory cannot be taken back once a process holds it. A container that goes over its memory limit is killed by the kernel's out-of-memory (OOM) killer. Kubernetes then shows `OOMKilled` and exit code 137. The 137 means the process got signal 9, SIGKILL (128 + 9).

A short way to remember it: too much CPU makes you slow, too much memory gets you killed.

The Deployment you update today asks for `100m` CPU and `128Mi` memory, and limits memory to `256Mi`. It sets no CPU limit on purpose. A CPU limit throttles a container even when the node has idle cores, which shows up as slow responses that are hard to explain. For a web app like this one, I would skip the CPU limit and rely on the request.

Requests are a different story: always set them. The scheduler, the autoscaler and the eviction order all depend on them. Skipping them is the first pitfall in the Kubernetes blog's [7 common pitfalls](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2025/10/20/seven-kubernetes-pitfalls-and-how-to-avoid/). One more rule from the docs: if you set a limit but no request, Kubernetes copies the limit into the request.

refs.title: Resource management for Pods and containers
Assign memory resources to containers and Pods
Kubernetes requests and limits (Tech Tutorials with Piyush, CKA series)

sections.body:
Your requests and limits also put each Pod into a quality of service (QoS) class. When a node runs short of memory, the kubelet evicts whole Pods to protect itself, and the class decides who goes first:
- BestEffort: no requests or limits at all. Evicted first.
- Burstable: at least one request or limit, but not Guaranteed. The lab's Pods are here.
- Guaranteed: every container has CPU and memory requests equal to its limits. Evicted last.

Eviction is different from an OOM kill. An OOM kill hits one container that broke its own limit. Eviction removes Pods because the node as a whole is short, and their Deployment recreates them on another node. Read a Pod's class with `kubectl get pod <name> -n hello -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}'`.

In a shared cluster, admins add two guard rails per namespace:
- A LimitRange sets default requests and limits for containers that set none, plus a minimum and maximum per container.
- A ResourceQuota caps the total for the whole namespace, such as 4 CPUs of requests, 8Gi of memory or 20 Pods.

With a quota on CPU or memory, the API server may reject any Pod that does not state those requests. A LimitRange with defaults fixes that for teams who forget. You will not need either on your laptop. You will meet both at work, often as an error message the first time you deploy to a new namespace.

A HorizontalPodAutoscaler (HPA) changes the number of replicas of a Deployment for you. It is one more control loop, like the ones from Day 30. Every 15 seconds it does this:
1. Reads the current CPU use of each Pod from the metrics API (more on that below).
2. Turns it into a percentage of the Pod's CPU request, and averages it.
3. Works out how many replicas would bring the average back to the target.
4. Sets the Deployment's replica count, between `minReplicas` and `maxReplicas`.

Step 3 is one line of math: `desired = ceil(currentReplicas * currentValue / targetValue)`. The lab's `k8s/hpa.yaml` targets 70% of the 100m request, so 70m per Pod. Say 3 Pods average 140m under load. That is twice the target, so the HPA asks for ceil(3 * 140 / 70) = 6 Pods. It ignores changes within 10% of the target, so the count does not jump around.

It scales up at once, but scales down slowly on purpose. By default it wants 5 minutes of lower numbers before it removes Pods. The lab shortens that to 2 minutes with `behavior.scaleDown.stabilizationWindowSeconds: 120`, so you can watch it happen.

The numbers come from metrics-server, a small add-on that asks each kubelet for CPU and memory use. kind does not ship it. After you install it, you add one flag, `--kubelet-insecure-tls`, because kind's kubelets use self-signed certificates. The [metrics-server README](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/metrics-server) says this flag is for testing only. Until metrics arrive, `kubectl get hpa` shows `cpu: <unknown>/70%`.

Three more rules. Without a CPU request the HPA cannot compute a percentage, so it does nothing. The Deployment's `replicas` field fights the HPA on every `kubectl apply`. The HPA docs suggest removing it; the lab keeps it equal to `minReplicas`, so the two agree when the app is quiet. And scale to zero exists since Kubernetes 1.37 as a beta, but only for object or external metrics such as a queue length, never for CPU.

refs.title: Kubernetes autoscaling explained: HPA vs VPA (Tech Tutorials with Piyush, CKA series)

sections.h: Scaling up: the VPA and in-place resize
sections.body:
The HPA adds Pods. The other direction is to make each Pod bigger, which is called vertical scaling.

The Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) watches real CPU and memory use over time and recommends requests. It is an add-on: you install its CRDs and controllers yourself, and it reads the same metrics API as the HPA. Its `updateMode` decides how far it goes:
- `Off`: only write recommendations. A safe way to learn what your app needs.
- `Initial`: set requests when Pods are created, never later.
- `Recreate`: evict Pods whose requests are far off, so they come back with new numbers.
- `InPlaceOrRecreate` and `InPlace`: change running Pods without a restart when the node allows it.

Do not let a VPA and an HPA both act on CPU for the same Deployment. The VPA raises the request, which lowers the HPA's percentage, and the two keep undoing each other's work.

Those last two modes rest on in-place Pod resize, which became stable in Kubernetes 1.35. Before it, a Pod's resources were fixed for its whole life. Now you can patch the `resize` subresource of a running Pod with `kubectl patch pod <name> --subresource resize --patch '...'`. Each container's `resizePolicy` says whether a change needs a restart. The default, `NotRequired`, applies the new numbers to the running container.

This works on single Pods. Changing the resources in a Deployment's template still rolls out new Pods, as on Day 32. Day to day you change the Deployment. In-place resize matters most for tools like the VPA, and for Pods that are slow or costly to restart.

refs.title: Resize CPU and memory resources assigned to containers

sections.h: Where Pods land, and how many may leave
sections.body:
The scheduler picks a node for each Pod from the nodes that fit its requests. You can steer that choice. From simple to strong:
1. `nodeSelector`: run only on nodes with this label, such as `disktype: ssd`.
2. Node affinity: the same idea with more operators. A `required` rule must match; a `preferred` rule is a wish the scheduler weighs.
3. Pod affinity and anti-affinity: place Pods near or away from other Pods, by their labels. Anti-affinity on `kubernetes.io/hostname`, a label every node has, spreads replicas over nodes.
4. Taints and tolerations: a taint on a node keeps Pods away, and a toleration on a Pod lets it in anyway.

You already have a taint. kind's control-plane node carries `node-role.kubernetes.io/control-plane:NoSchedule`. That is why your app Pods only ever land on the two workers. `kubectl describe node devops-control-plane | grep Taints` shows it. The prod overlay on Day 37 uses anti-affinity, so one node failure is less likely to take every Pod.

Last, the PodDisruptionBudget (PDB). Kubernetes splits disruptions into two kinds. Voluntary ones are planned, such as a `kubectl drain` before node maintenance, or a cluster upgrade. Involuntary ones just happen: a node crashes or loses power. A PDB limits only the voluntary kind.

With `minAvailable: 2`, a drain evicts hello-devops Pods one at a time. Each eviction waits until enough replacements are ready elsewhere, so at least 2 keep serving. A PDB cannot stop a crash. Replicas spread over several nodes are your answer to that.

lessons.analogy: A shop manager checks a new clerk in three ways. On the first morning she gives them time to settle in before judging anything: that is the startup probe. Every few minutes she checks that they are awake at all, and if not, sends them home and calls someone new: liveness. And she checks whether they can serve customers right now; if their till is broken, she puts a closed sign on that counter but keeps the clerk: readiness. Where it breaks: the manager can ask why, while the kubelet only sees pass or fail from one URL.

worked.title: Cause an OOMKill and read the evidence

steps.say: Start a Pod that grabs 150 MB of memory but may use only 100Mi. It runs Python from the hello-devops image, which your kind nodes already have, so nothing is downloaded.
steps.code:
$ kubectl apply -n hello -f - <<'EOF'
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: hog
spec:
  containers:
    - name: hog
      image: hello-devops:1.0.0
      command: ["python", "-c", "import time; data = bytearray(150 * 1024 * 1024); print('got 150 MB'); time.sleep(3600)"]
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 100Mi
EOF
pod/hog created

steps.say: Watch it. Within seconds the kernel kills it. Kubernetes restarts it, it dies again, and the waits between restarts grow: that is `CrashLoopBackOff`. Press Ctrl+C to stop watching.
steps.code:
$ kubectl get pod hog -n hello -w
NAME   READY   STATUS              RESTARTS     AGE
hog    0/1     ContainerCreating   0            1s
hog    0/1     OOMKilled           0            3s
hog    0/1     OOMKilled           1 (2s ago)   5s
hog    0/1     CrashLoopBackOff    1 (3s ago)   6s

steps.say: `describe` keeps the reason of the last crash under Last State. `OOMKilled` with exit code 137 means the kernel sent SIGKILL because the container went over its memory limit.
steps.code:
$ kubectl describe pod hog -n hello | grep -A 3 "Last State"
    Last State:     Terminated
      Reason:       OOMKilled
      Exit Code:    137
      Started:      Fri, 30 Oct 2026 10:12:03 +0000

steps.say: The crashed container's log is empty. Python never reached its print line, and a process killed from outside gets no chance to write an error. An empty log plus exit code 137 points at memory, not at your code.
steps.code:
$ kubectl logs hog -n hello --previous
$

steps.say: Look at what Kubernetes stored. You set only a memory limit, so it copied the limit into the memory request. With no CPU numbers at all, the Pod is Burstable, not Guaranteed.
steps.code:
$ kubectl get pod hog -n hello -o jsonpath='{.spec.containers[0].resources}{"\n"}'
{"limits":{"memory":"100Mi"},"requests":{"memory":"100Mi"}}
$ kubectl get pod hog -n hello -o jsonpath='{.status.qosClass}{"\n"}'
Burstable

steps.say: Fix it. A bare Pod's resources only change through the resize subresource, so the simple path is delete and recreate. Run the command from step 1 again with `memory: 256Mi`. A Deployment would do this replace for you.
steps.code:
$ kubectl delete pod hog -n hello
pod "hog" deleted from hello namespace
$ # run the command from step 1 again, with memory: 256Mi
$ kubectl get pod hog -n hello
NAME   READY   STATUS    RESTARTS   AGE
hog    1/1     Running   0          8s
$ kubectl logs hog -n hello
got 150 MB

steps.say: Clean up. In real work you would pick the new limit from measured use, with `kubectl top pod`.
steps.code:
$ kubectl delete pod hog -n hello
pod "hog" deleted from hello namespace

code.title: k8s/deployment.yaml (final version: Day 35 adds the probes and resources)
code.src:
# Runs 3 copies (pods) of hello-devops and replaces any that die.
# Day 32 writes the first version, Day 34 adds envFrom, Day 35 adds the probes and resources.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  namespace: hello
  labels:
    app: hello-devops
spec:
  replicas: 3 # equal to minReplicas in hpa.yaml, so the two agree when the app is quiet
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: hello-devops # must match the pod labels below
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate:
      maxUnavailable: 0 # never drop below 3 ready pods during an update
      maxSurge: 1 # add at most 1 extra pod at a time
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello-devops
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: hello-devops:1.0.0
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent # use the image kind loaded; do not pull it
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8000
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef:
                name: hello-config # every key in the ConfigMap becomes an env var
          startupProbe: # gives a slow start up to 30 x 2s = 60s
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 30
          livenessProbe: # fails 3 times in a row: restart the container
            httpGet:
              path: /healthz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 10
          readinessProbe: # fails 2 times in a row: stop sending traffic to this pod
            httpGet:
              path: /readyz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5
            timeoutSeconds: 2
            failureThreshold: 2
          resources:
            requests: # what the scheduler reserves for this container
              cpu: 100m
              memory: 128Mi
            limits: # the most it may use; over the memory limit it is killed
              memory: 256Mi

# Adds or removes hello-devops Pods to keep average CPU near 70% of the request.
# Needs metrics-server in the cluster (Day 35 shows how to install it on kind).
apiVersion: autoscaling/v2
kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  namespace: hello
spec:
  scaleTargetRef:
    apiVersion: apps/v1
    kind: Deployment
    name: hello-devops
  minReplicas: 3 # the same as replicas in deployment.yaml, so the two agree when the app is quiet
  maxReplicas: 6
  metrics:
    - type: Resource
      resource:
        name: cpu
        target:
          type: Utilization
          averageUtilization: 70 # 70% of the CPU request (100m), so about 70m per Pod
  behavior:
    scaleDown:
      stabilizationWindowSeconds: 120 # wait for 2 quiet minutes before removing Pods (the default is 300)

An HPA adds checkout Pods as traffic climbs during sales, and a PDB lets node upgrades take down only one checkout Pod at a time. Probe changes go through code review like alert rules, because a bad liveness probe can restart every Pod at once.

task.title: Probes, autoscaling and a safe drain on the lab app
steps: Add the three probes and the resources to `k8s/deployment.yaml` (the file above) and apply with `kubectl apply -k k8s`. Work out from the timing settings how long each probe takes to act, and check the probes in `kubectl describe pod`.
In a second terminal, run `kubectl get pods -n hello -w`. Scale Redis to 0 replicas and watch the hello-devops Pods go to `0/1` READY while RESTARTS stays at 0. Try `curl localhost:8081`.
Scale Redis back to 1 and watch the app Pods become ready again on their own.
Install metrics-server, add the `--kubelet-insecure-tls` flag, and wait until `kubectl top pods -n hello` prints numbers.
Write `k8s/hpa.yaml`, add it to `k8s/kustomization.yaml`, and apply with `kubectl apply -k k8s`. Check that `kubectl get hpa -n hello` shows a real percentage instead of `<unknown>`.

Start the load generator Pod from the commands list and watch `kubectl get hpa -n hello -w` until REPLICAS goes above 3. Delete the load Pod and watch the count return to 3 after about 2 quiet minutes.
Create a PodDisruptionBudget for hello-devops with `minAvailable` 2 and read ALLOWED DISRUPTIONS in `kubectl get pdb -n hello`.

Print the QoS class of one hello-devops Pod and of the Redis Pod, and explain each from their resources.

The drain needs `--ignore-daemonsets` (kindnet and kube-proxy run on every node) and `--delete-emptydir-data` (metrics-server keeps scratch files in an emptyDir).

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences why the hello-devops Pods went to 0/1 READY but did not restart when you scaled Redis to zero. Mention both probes and what each one checks.
explain_back.answer: The readiness probe calls `/readyz`, which pings Redis, so it started returning 503 and the Pods left the Service's endpoints. The liveness probe calls `/healthz`, which only checks that the process answers, so it kept passing and the kubelet had no reason to restart anything. When Redis came back, `/readyz` passed again and the Pods rejoined the Service without anyone touching them. If liveness had checked Redis, every Pod would have restarted for nothing.

recap: Startup holds back the other probes, liveness restarts a stuck container, readiness only stops traffic.
Keep dependencies out of liveness; a shared outage would restart every Pod at once.
Requests decide placement; over the memory limit means OOMKilled (exit 137), at the CPU limit means throttling.
Requests and limits set the QoS class, which decides eviction order when a node runs short.
An HPA needs metrics-server (with `--kubelet-insecure-tls` on kind) and CPU requests; it scales up fast and down slowly.
Taints, affinity and nodeSelector steer scheduling; a PDB limits planned disruptions such as a drain.

check.q: A Spring Boot service needs about 90 seconds to start. Its liveness probe kills it after 30 seconds, again and again. What is the best fix?
options: Add a startup probe that allows more than 90 seconds
Raise the container's memory limit
Point the readiness probe at `/healthz` too
Add more replicas to the Deployment
check.why: A startup probe holds the liveness probe back until the app has started, so slow starts are not mistaken for a stuck process.

check.q: metrics-server works and `kubectl top pods` prints numbers, but the HPA still shows `cpu: <unknown>/70%`. What is the most likely cause?
options: The HPA needs a memory metric as well
The cluster has too few worker nodes
The Pods have no CPU request to compute a percentage from
The Deployment's `replicas` is set higher than `maxReplicas`
check.why: A utilization target is a percentage of the CPU request, so without a request the HPA has nothing to divide by.

check.q: A Deployment has 3 replicas and a PDB with `minAvailable: 3`. You run `kubectl drain` on the node that holds one of them. What happens?
options: The Pod is evicted at once, and the PDB is ignored for drains
The node is deleted and the Pod moves with it
Kubernetes adds a fourth replica first, then evicts
The eviction is refused and drain keeps retrying
check.why: With all 3 required, the budget allows 0 disruptions, so every eviction is refused until you change the PDB or add replicas.

interview.q: What is the difference between liveness, readiness and startup probes?
interview.a: A liveness probe checks whether the container is stuck; after repeated failures the kubelet restarts it. A readiness probe checks whether the Pod can take traffic; while it fails, the Pod is removed from Service endpoints but keeps running. A startup probe protects slow starters by holding the other two back until it passes. Liveness should test only the process itself, while readiness may check dependencies such as a database.

interview.q: How do requests and limits work, and what happens when a container goes over them?
interview.a: Requests are what the scheduler reserves, so they decide which node a Pod can go on, and the HPA computes percentages from them. Limits are the most a container may use, enforced by the kernel through cgroups. Over the memory limit the container is OOMKilled with exit code 137; at the CPU limit it is only throttled. I always set requests and a memory limit, and think twice before adding a CPU limit to a latency-sensitive service.

interview.q: An HPA is not scaling. How do you find out why?
interview.a: First `kubectl get hpa` to see the current value: `<unknown>` means no metrics, so check that metrics-server runs and that the Pods have CPU requests. Then `kubectl describe hpa` shows conditions such as AbleToScale and ScalingActive, plus events that explain each decision. If metrics look fine, check whether the count is already at `maxReplicas`, or whether the target is so high that the load never crosses it. Last, look for a second controller, such as a VPA on CPU or a deploy tool resetting `replicas`.

deeper.body:
Picking good numbers is most of the work with resources, and guessing goes wrong in both directions. Requests that are too high waste nodes and make the HPA react late, because each Pod looks idle. Requests that are too low pack too many Pods onto a node and make the HPA scale early and often.

A simple way to start from data:
1. Run the app under normal load for a day and look at its use with `kubectl top pods`, or a Grafana dashboard once you reach Part 10.
2. Set the memory request near normal use and the memory limit with room for peaks, often about twice the request.
3. Set the CPU request near normal use. The HPA's percentage is based on it, so this number also sets when scaling starts.
4. Run a VPA in `Off` mode next to the app. Its recommendations are a second opinion that costs nothing.
5. Check again after big changes to the app, such as a new framework version or a new cache.

CPU is not always the right signal to scale on. A worker that reads jobs from a queue may sit at low CPU while thousands of jobs wait. KEDA, a CNCF project, scales Deployments on events such as queue length, and can scale to zero when there is no work. Kubernetes 1.37 also lets an HPA scale to zero by itself as a beta, when it uses an object or external metric.

All of this scales Pods. When the nodes are full, new Pods stay `Pending`. Node autoscalers, such as the Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter on a cloud, notice those Pending Pods and add nodes. When nodes are under-used, they drain and remove them, and that drain respects your PDBs. A kind cluster cannot add nodes, so on your laptop the ceiling is the memory you gave Docker Desktop.

Probes deserve the same care as numbers. Tune them like alerts: a probe acts on its own, often when nobody is watching. Before you tighten a timeout, ask what happens if every Pod fails that probe in the same minute.

lessons.goal: By the end you can route outside traffic to hello-devops through a Gateway, send a small share of it to a canary, end TLS at the Gateway, and give a Pod storage that outlives it.

options: Traffic starts flowing, because Kubernetes ships a default proxy
Kubernetes downloads Envoy and starts it for you
The objects are saved, and the old Ingress controller serves them
The apply fails, because the cluster does not know these object types
guess.why: The Gateway API is not built in. Until you install its CRDs, the API server rejects the objects with "no matches for kind", and even then nothing routes until a controller such as Envoy Gateway runs.

terms.plain: The older Kubernetes object for HTTP routing into a cluster; its API is now frozen.
The newer official routing objects (GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute), installed as CRDs.
An entry point with listeners, such as HTTP on port 80, run by a proxy that a controller starts.
Rules that match requests by path, header or host and send them to Services, with optional weights.
An app's request for storage of a given size and access mode.
A piece of real storage in the cluster that a claim binds to.
A type of storage the cluster can create on demand when a claim asks for it.
Like a Deployment, but each Pod keeps a stable name and its own volume.

sections.body:
So far you have reached hello-devops in two ways: the NodePort that kind maps to localhost:8081 (Day 33), and `kubectl port-forward`. Both are fine on a laptop. Neither is how real users arrive.

Traffic that enters the cluster from outside is called north-south traffic. Traffic between Services inside the cluster is east-west. For north-south HTTP traffic you usually want:
- One entry point for many apps, so you pay for one load balancer instead of ten.
- Routing by host name and path, such as `shop.example.com/api` to one Service and `/` to another.
- TLS in one place, so each app does not handle its own certificates.
- Gradual releases, such as sending 10% of requests to a new version.

A Service of type LoadBalancer gives you an address, but it works with connections (layer 4). It never looks at a URL path or a header. For that you need a proxy that understands HTTP (layer 7), plus a Kubernetes object that tells the proxy what to do. Kubernetes has two such APIs: the older Ingress and the newer Gateway API.

refs.title: What is Gateway API for Kubernetes? Find out in ten minutes

sections.h: Ingress, and why it is fading
sections.body:
An Ingress is a Kubernetes object with HTTP routing rules: host names, paths and the Service each one goes to. It has been stable since Kubernetes 1.19, and you will see it in many clusters and tutorials. An Ingress does nothing by itself. An Ingress controller, a proxy running in the cluster, reads the objects and does the routing.

Two things changed:
- The Ingress API is frozen. It stays supported, but it gets no new features, and the [Ingress docs](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/services-networking/ingress/) recommend Gateway instead.
- ingress-nginx, the most popular community controller, was retired on March 24, 2026. Existing installs keep running, with no more releases, bug fixes or security patches.

Ingress was small on purpose: hosts, paths and TLS. Everything else, such as rewrites, timeouts or canary weights, went into annotations that each controller defined its own way. A config written for one controller rarely worked on another.

If you meet ingress-nginx at work, treat it as a migration. `kubectl get pods -A -l app.kubernetes.io/name=ingress-nginx` finds it. [Ingress2Gateway](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/03/20/ingress2gateway-1-0-release/) translates Ingress objects and many ingress-nginx annotations into Gateway API objects, and warns about what it cannot translate. Do not confuse ingress-nginx with F5's NGINX Ingress Controller, which is a separate product.

refs.title: Ingress NGINX retirement: what you need to know
Before you migrate: five surprising Ingress-NGINX behaviors

sections.h: The Gateway API: one object per role
sections.body:
The **Gateway API** is the newer, official set of objects for routing traffic into a cluster. It is not built into Kubernetes. You install it as CRDs (custom resource definitions: new object types that the API server learns), plus a controller that implements them. Until the CRDs exist, applying a Gateway fails with "no matches for kind".

It splits the job by who owns what:
- GatewayClass: which controller handles Gateways of this class. The platform team creates it once per cluster.
- Gateway: an entry point with one or more listeners, such as "HTTP on port 80". The controller starts a proxy for it.
- HTTPRoute: routing rules for one app, such as "`/` goes to Service `hello-devops` on port 80". App teams own these and attach them to a Gateway.

A Gateway's `allowedRoutes` decides which namespaces may attach routes. The lab allows all of them, which is easy on a laptop. At work you would pick `Same` or a label selector.

Features that Ingress hid in annotations are real fields here: header matching, weights, redirects, rewrites and timeouts. Because they are fields, they behave the same across implementations such as Envoy Gateway, Istio, Cilium, Traefik and the cloud providers' load balancers.

The Gateway API ships on its own schedule, separate from Kubernetes. Version 1.7 is the newest. Each release has a Standard channel (stable) and an Experimental channel. Stick to Standard: everything in this lesson has been Standard since 1.0.

refs.title: Mastering Kubernetes Gateway API (Is it Observable)

sections.h: Envoy Gateway on kind, step by step
sections.body:
To try it you need one implementation. This course uses Envoy Gateway, an open source controller that runs the Envoy proxy (Envoy itself is a CNCF project). One `helm install` brings the controller and its own copy of the Gateway API CRDs. Envoy Gateway 1.9 bundles Gateway API 1.6, which is fine, because the lab uses only Standard features.

When you run `kubectl apply -k k8s/gateway`, this happens:
1. The GatewayClass `eg` names the controller `gateway.envoyproxy.io/gatewayclass-controller`. Envoy Gateway sees its own name and accepts the class.
2. The Gateway `hello-gateway` uses class `eg`, so Envoy Gateway creates an Envoy proxy Deployment and Service for it in `envoy-gateway-system`.
3. The HTTPRoute `hello-devops` attaches to `hello-gateway` and points at the `hello-devops` Service.
4. Envoy Gateway turns the route into Envoy settings and sends them to the proxy, which starts forwarding.

kind has one catch. The proxy's Service has type LoadBalancer. On a cloud, that creates a real load balancer with an address. A kind cluster has no cloud, so the Service never gets one. As a result, `kubectl get gateway -n hello` shows PROGRAMMED `False` with the message "No addresses have been assigned to the Gateway". This is expected. The routing behind it works, and you reach the proxy with `kubectl port-forward`, as the [Envoy Gateway quickstart](https://gateway.envoyproxy.io/docs/tasks/quickstart/) does.

If you want a real address on kind, a small tool called [cloud-provider-kind](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/cloud-provider-kind) acts as a cloud load balancer for kind clusters. On a Mac it exposes the address through a port on localhost. For one app on a laptop, port-forward is enough.

refs.title: Experimenting with Gateway API using kind (Kubernetes blog)

sections.body:
An HTTPRoute holds a list of rules, and each rule has matches and backends. A match can test:
- The path, such as `PathPrefix /api` or `Exact /healthz`.
- Headers, such as `x-canary: always`.
- The HTTP method and query parameters.

When several rules match one request, the most specific one wins. A longer path beats a shorter one, and with equal paths, more header matches win. You do not need to order rules by hand.

A rule can send traffic to more than one backend, with weights. Weights 90 and 10 send about 9 of every 10 requests to the first Service and 1 to the second. That is a canary release: a new version gets a small share of real traffic while you watch its errors and latency. If it looks good, you move the weights. If not, you set the canary to 0. The lab's `k8s/gateway/httproute-canary.yaml` does this, and adds a header rule so testers can always reach the canary.

TLS is set on the Gateway, not on each route. An HTTPS listener with `tls.mode: Terminate` decrypts at the proxy, with a certificate and key from a Secret of type `kubernetes.io/tls`. The proxy then sends plain HTTP to your Pods inside the cluster. Apps stay simple, and one team manages certificates in one place. At work, cert-manager usually creates and renews those Secrets. In the lab you make a self-signed certificate with `openssl`, so `curl` needs `-k` to accept it.

Containers lose their files when they restart, because each start begins again from the image. A volume is a folder that Kubernetes mounts into a container. Some volumes are short-lived: an `emptyDir` is created with its Pod and deleted with it. It suits scratch files and sharing files between containers in one Pod.

For data that must survive the Pod, there are three objects:
- A **PersistentVolume** (PV) is a piece of real storage: a cloud disk, a network share or a folder on a node.
- A PersistentVolumeClaim (PVC) is an app's request for storage: "1Gi that one node can read and write".
- A StorageClass is a type of storage the cluster can create on demand.

You mostly write PVCs. When a PVC names a StorageClass, or the cluster has a default one, the class's provisioner creates a matching PV. That is called dynamic provisioning. kind's default class is called `standard`. It uses the local-path provisioner, which makes a folder on a node. Two of its settings matter:
- `volumeBindingMode: WaitForFirstConsumer`: the PV is created only when a Pod uses the claim, on that Pod's node.
- `reclaimPolicy: Delete`: deleting the PVC also deletes the PV and the data.

Access modes say who may mount a volume. The mode `ReadWriteOnce` (RWO) means one node at a time, the usual case for disks. The mode `ReadWriteMany` (RWX) needs network storage such as NFS. Two more modes exist: `ReadOnlyMany` and `ReadWriteOncePod`.

sections.h: StatefulSets, and why managed databases often win
sections.body:
A Deployment treats its Pods as interchangeable. They get random names, and any one can replace any other. A database cannot work like that: replica 0 might be the primary, and each replica needs its own disk.

A StatefulSet gives each Pod:
- A stable name with a number, such as `redis-0` and `redis-1`.
- Its own PVC from a `volumeClaimTemplates` section, such as `data-redis-0`. A replacement Pod gets the same PVC back.
- A stable DNS name through a headless Service (Day 33), such as `redis-0.redis.hello.svc.cluster.local`.
- Ordered start and stop: `redis-0` first, then `redis-1`.

Deleting a StatefulSet does not delete its PVCs. That protects your data, and it means you clean up by hand.

You can run databases this way. Operators (controllers built for one database, such as CloudNativePG for Postgres) automate a lot of the work. Still, backups, upgrades, replication and failover become your job. Many teams keep the cluster for stateless apps and pay for a managed database such as Amazon RDS or Cloud SQL. My rule of thumb: if losing the data would hurt the business, start with a managed database, and move it into the cluster only for a real reason. The lab's Redis has no volume at all, because it only holds a demo counter. Go deeper below to give it one.

lessons.analogy: The Gateway is the reception desk of an office building, and the GatewayClass is the company that staffs it. Each HTTPRoute is a line in the visitor book that a tenant writes: "visitors for Acme go to floor 3, testers with a blue badge go to floor 4". Tenants add their own lines without touching the desk. Where it breaks: a receptionist can use judgment, while the proxy follows the most specific matching rule and nothing else.

code.title: k8s/gateway/kustomization.yaml
code.src:
# The Gateway API front door for hello-devops (Day 36). Apply with: kubectl apply -k k8s/gateway
# Install Envoy Gateway first: it brings the Gateway API types (CRDs) and the controller.
# Not listed here on purpose: canary.yaml, httproute-canary.yaml and gateway-https.yaml
# are optional extras that you apply by hand with kubectl apply -f.

  - gateway.yaml
  - httproute.yaml

code.title: k8s/gateway/gatewayclass.yaml

# Which controller runs our Gateways: Envoy Gateway. Cluster-wide, so no namespace.

metadata:

  namespace: hello
spec:

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello-canary
  namespace: hello
  labels:
    app: hello-canary
spec:
  replicas: 1

    matchLabels:
      app: hello-canary

    metadata:
      labels:
        app: hello-canary
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: web
          image: hello-devops:1.0.0
          imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
          ports:
            - name: http
              containerPort: 8000

            - name: APP_VERSION
              value: "1.1.0-canary"
            - name: GREETING
              value: "Hello from the canary!"
            - name: REDIS_HOST
              value: "redis" # share the visit counter with the main app
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet:
              path: /readyz
              port: http
            periodSeconds: 5

            requests:
              cpu: 50m
              memory: 128Mi
            limits:

---

kind: Service
metadata:
  name: hello-canary
  namespace: hello

code.title: k8s/gateway/httproute-canary.yaml
code.src:
# A canary release. It has the same name as httproute.yaml, so applying it REPLACES that route.
#   kubectl apply -f k8s/gateway/httproute-canary.yaml   (start the canary)
#   kubectl apply -k k8s/gateway                         (go back to 100% hello-devops)
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
  namespace: hello
spec:
  parentRefs:
    - name: hello-gateway
  rules:
    # Rule 1: requests with the header "x-canary: always" always go to the canary.
    # A header match is more specific than a path alone, so this rule wins for those requests.
    - matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /
          headers:
            - name: x-canary
              value: always
      backendRefs:
        - name: hello-canary
          port: 80
    # Rule 2: everyone else. About 9 in 10 requests go to hello-devops, 1 in 10 to the canary.
    - matches:
        - path:
            type: PathPrefix
            value: /
      backendRefs:
        - name: hello-devops
          port: 80
          weight: 90
        - name: hello-canary
          port: 80
          weight: 10

# Optional (Day 36): the same Gateway as gateway.yaml, plus an HTTPS listener on port 443.
# The Gateway ends TLS here and sends plain HTTP to the Pods ("TLS termination").
# First create the Secret "hello-tls" from a certificate and key, then:
#   kubectl apply -f k8s/gateway/gateway-https.yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: hello-gateway
  namespace: hello
spec:
  gatewayClassName: eg
  listeners:
    - name: http
      protocol: HTTP
      port: 80
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces:
          from: All
    - name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
      port: 443
      tls:
        mode: Terminate # decrypt at the Gateway
        certificateRefs:
          - kind: Secret
            name: hello-tls # a Secret of type kubernetes.io/tls in namespace hello
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces:
          from: All

# Day 36 storage demo: a claim for a small disk, and a Pod that writes to it.
# Apply with: kubectl apply -f k8s/storage/pvc-demo.yaml
# Clean up with: kubectl delete namespace storage-demo
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: storage-demo
---
# The claim: "I need 1Gi that one node can read and write."
# No storageClassName, so the cluster's default class is used (on kind: "standard").
apiVersion: v1
kind: PersistentVolumeClaim
metadata:
  name: notes
  namespace: storage-demo
spec:
  accessModes:
    - ReadWriteOnce
  resources:
    requests:
      storage: 1Gi
---
# Each time this Pod starts, it adds one line to /data/starts.log and prints the whole file.
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: writer
  namespace: storage-demo
spec:
  containers:
    - name: writer
      image: busybox:1.37
      command: ["sh", "-c", "echo \"started at $(date)\" >> /data/starts.log; cat /data/starts.log; sleep 3600"]
      volumeMounts:
        - name: notes
          mountPath: /data # the disk appears here inside the container
      resources:
        requests:
          cpu: 10m
          memory: 16Mi
        limits:
          memory: 32Mi
  volumes:
    - name: notes
      persistentVolumeClaim:
        claimName: notes # use the claim above

steps: Install Envoy Gateway with Helm (check its quickstart for the current version) and wait until the `envoy-gateway` Deployment is Available.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences how one `curl localhost:8888` request can end up at the canary Pod. Mention the Gateway, the HTTPRoute, the weights and the Service.
explain_back.answer: Port-forward sends the request to the Envoy proxy that Envoy Gateway started for `hello-gateway`. Envoy checks the HTTPRoutes attached to that Gateway; my request has no `x-canary` header, so the 90/10 rule matches. check.q: A shop needs `/api` sent to Service `api` and every other path to Service `web`, through one Gateway. What do you write?
options: A second GatewayClass for the API traffic
Two Gateways, one for each Service
An HTTPRoute with two rules that match on path
A LoadBalancer Service with two ports
check.why: Routing rules live in an HTTPRoute; the `/api` prefix rule is more specific, so it wins for those requests and `/` takes the rest.

check.q: On kind, `kubectl get gateway` shows PROGRAMMED False, "No addresses have been assigned", but curl through the port-forward works. What should you fix?
options: Nothing: kind has no cloud load balancer to give the Gateway an address
The HTTPRoute, because it did not attach to the Gateway
The GatewayClass, because its controller name is wrong
The Service, because its targetPort does not match
check.why: Programmed is False only because the proxy's LoadBalancer Service never got an address; routing works, as the curl shows.

check.q: A Postgres Pod on kind keeps its data on a PVC from the `standard` class. You delete the whole namespace. What happens to the data?
options: It stays on the PV until you delete the PV by hand
It is deleted, because the class's reclaim policy is Delete
It is saved into etcd until a new claim asks for it
It moves to another node with free space
check.why: Deleting the namespace deletes the PVC, and with `reclaimPolicy: Delete` the PV and its folder go too.

interview.q: Why is the Gateway API replacing Ingress?
interview.a: Ingress covered only hosts, paths and TLS, so every controller added its own annotations, and configs did not move between controllers. The Gateway API makes features such as header matching, weights and timeouts real fields that behave the same everywhere. It also splits ownership: the platform team runs GatewayClasses and Gateways, and app teams write Routes. On top of that, the Ingress API is frozen and ingress-nginx was retired in March 2026, so new clusters should start with Gateway API.

interview.q: Explain PV, PVC and StorageClass, and how dynamic provisioning works.
interview.a: A PVC is an app's request for storage, a PV is the actual storage, and a StorageClass describes a kind of storage and the provisioner that creates it. With dynamic provisioning, the app only writes a PVC; the class's provisioner creates a matching PV and the two are bound. The binding mode decides when that happens, often only once a Pod is scheduled, and the reclaim policy decides whether the data is deleted or kept with the claim. Access modes such as ReadWriteOnce limit how many nodes can mount it at once.

interview.q: Would you run your database in Kubernetes?
interview.a: It depends on the team and the data. A StatefulSet gives stable names and one volume per replica, and operators such as CloudNativePG automate failover and backups. But the team then owns backups, restores, upgrades and capacity, and has to test them. For business-critical data and a small team, I would start with a managed database and keep the cluster for stateless services and caches. I would move a database in only for a clear reason, such as cost at scale or a platform team that already runs operators well.

deeper.body:
The lab's Redis forgets the visit count every time its Pod restarts. A StatefulSet with a volume fixes that. Treat these steps as a sketch to try in a copy of `k8s/redis.yaml`, not as a change to the base:
1. Change `kind: Deployment` to `kind: StatefulSet`, and add `serviceName: redis` under `spec`.
2. Add a `volumeClaimTemplates` section with one template named `data`: access mode `ReadWriteOnce` and a request of `1Gi`. The StatefulSet makes one PVC per Pod, called `data-redis-0`.
3. Mount the `data` volume at `/data` in the Redis container. The official Redis image keeps its files there.
4. Turn on saving: run Redis with `redis-server --appendonly yes`, so each write also goes to disk.
5. Apply it, count a few visits, then delete the Pod `redis-0`. It comes back with the same name and the same PVC, and the count carries on.

Check the pieces with `kubectl get pvc -n hello` and `kubectl get pv`. On kind the PV is a folder inside a node container, so deleting the cluster deletes the data. For practice that is fine.

Things that surprise people:
- Deleting a StatefulSet leaves its PVCs behind. You delete them yourself when you are sure.
- A local-path volume lives on one node, so `redis-0` can only ever be scheduled there. If that node goes away, the Pod stays `Pending`. A cloud disk can attach to another node; a local folder cannot.
- A StatefulSet wants a headless Service (`clusterIP: None`) so each Pod gets its own DNS name. Your existing `redis` Service is a normal one; for one replica that still works.
- Scaling down does not delete the PVCs of removed Pods, so scaling back up finds the old data.

Kubernetes 1.37 also changed two StatefulSet details you may read about. The `maxUnavailable` setting for rolling updates is on by default again. A new `Recreate` update strategy exists as an alpha feature.

The traffic side has its own next step. cloud-provider-kind can give the Gateway a real address on your laptop. It runs on your Mac, watches the cluster, and exposes each LoadBalancer Service through a port on localhost. With it running, `kubectl get gateway` shows an address and PROGRAMMED True, which matches what you will see on a cloud. Read its README before you install it, because it needs permission to open ports on your machine.

terms.plain: A package of templated Kubernetes YAML plus default values, in one folder.
The settings that fill a chart's templates, from values.yaml, -f files or --set.
One installed copy of a chart in a namespace, with its own name.
One numbered version of a release; every install, upgrade or rollback adds one.
A tool built into kubectl that builds YAML from a base plus changes, without templates.
A Kustomize folder that points at a base and lists the changes for one environment.
A small description of changes to an object, applied on top of the base.
A registry such as ghcr.io that stores images, and also Helm charts.

sections.body:
hello-devops now has more than ten YAML files. Imagine running it three times, for dev, staging and prod. Each copy needs a different image tag, replica count and greeting, and prod also wants a disruption budget. If you copy the folder three times, the copies drift apart. Someone fixes a probe in prod and forgets dev. Six months later, nobody knows which differences are on purpose.

There are two popular answers, and they come from opposite directions:
- Templating, with Helm: write the YAML once with blanks, such as `replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}`, and fill the blanks per environment from a values file.
- Patching, with Kustomize: keep plain, valid YAML as a base, and describe each environment as a small set of changes on top of it.

Both end the same way. They render ordinary Kubernetes YAML, and the API server never knows which tool made it. That is also why Argo CD (Day 39) can deploy with either one.

You will use both at work, often in the same cluster. Helm is how most third-party software ships. Kustomize is a common choice for a team's own services. This lesson builds one of each for hello-devops.
