sections.h: A Helm chart from the inside
sections.body:
Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes, a bit like Homebrew for apps in a cluster. A package is called a **chart**, and a chart is a folder:
- `Chart.yaml`: the chart's name, its own `version`, and the `appVersion` it deploys by default.
- `values.yaml`: the default settings.
- `templates/`: YAML files with placeholders in Go template syntax.
- `templates/_helpers.tpl`: named snippets that other templates reuse. Files that start with `_` render no objects.
- `templates/NOTES.txt`: text Helm prints after an install, such as how to reach the app.

Inside a template, `{{ .Values.greeting }}` reads a value, `{{ .Release.Name }}` is the name you gave this install, and `{{ .Chart.AppVersion }}` comes from `Chart.yaml`. A pipe changes a value: `{{ .Values.greeting | quote }}` wraps it in quotes. A line such as `{{- if .Values.httpRoute.enabled }}` leaves a whole object out unless the value is true. The `-` trims the blank line the tag would leave.

The lab chart puts the same labels on every object with one helper: `{{- include "hello-devops.labels" . | nindent 4 }}`. The `include` function renders the helper, and `nindent 4` starts a new line indented by 4 spaces, which YAML needs. Indentation is where most template bugs come from, so render before you install. `helm template hello chart/hello-devops` prints the final YAML, and `helm lint` checks the chart for mistakes. Neither touches the cluster.

The chart also has a small trick from the [Helm tips page](https://helm.sh/docs/howto/charts_tips_and_tricks/). A `checksum/config` annotation on the Pod template holds a hash of the ConfigMap. Change the greeting, the hash changes, and the Deployment rolls out new Pods that read it.

refs.title: What is Helm in Kubernetes? Helm and Helm charts explained (TechWorld with Nana; its Tiller part is Helm 2 history)

sections.body:
When you install a chart, Helm creates a release: one named copy of the chart in one namespace. You can install the same chart many times under different names. Every install, upgrade or rollback adds a numbered revision, and Helm stores each revision as a Secret in the release's namespace.

The commands follow a release's life:
1. `helm install hello chart/hello-devops -f chart/kind-values.yaml` renders with your values, applies, and records revision 1.
2. `helm upgrade hello chart/hello-devops -f chart/kind-values.yaml` renders again and applies the difference as revision 2.
3. `helm history hello` lists the revisions and their status.
4. `helm rollback hello 1` applies what revision 1 had, recorded as a new revision 3. History is never rewritten.
5. `helm uninstall hello` deletes every object the release created.

`helm upgrade --install` installs when the release does not exist yet and upgrades when it does. CI pipelines use it so one command works both times.

One rule surprises nearly everyone. If you pass any values on `helm upgrade`, Helm starts from the chart's defaults plus only the values you pass now. Values you passed at install time are dropped. With no values at all, it reuses the last ones. So keep your settings in a values file and pass it with `-f` every time.

By default, `helm install` returns once the API server has the objects, before the Pods are ready. Add `--wait` to wait for them, and `--rollback-on-failure` to undo an upgrade that fails.

refs.title: Using Helm: install, upgrade and rollback

sections.body:
Helm 4.0 came out in November 2025, the first major version in six years. Day to day it feels like Helm 3, and charts with `apiVersion: v2` work unchanged. A few changes matter to you:
- Server-side apply is the default for new releases. The API server merges the changes and tracks which tool owns each field. Upgrades and rollbacks keep the method the release started with, so old Helm 3 releases stay on client-side apply.
- Two flags were renamed: `--atomic` is now `--rollback-on-failure`, and `--force` is now `--force-replace`. The old names still work but print a warning, and older blog posts use them.
- `--wait` uses kstatus, a status library, to tell when each kind of object is ready.
- You can install a chart by digest, `oci://...@sha256:...`, so you get exactly the bytes you tested.
- Post-renderers are now plugins, and `helm registry login` takes only the host name.

Helm 3 is at the end of its life. Its last feature release came out on September 9, 2026, and its security fixes stop on February 10, 2027. Install Helm 4 and learn its flag names.

A new chart format, Charts v3, is experimental and hidden behind `HELM_EXPERIMENTAL_CHART_V3=1`. You can ignore it for now.

You can share a chart through the same kind of registry that stores your images. Helm calls this OCI support, after the Open Container Initiative standard that registries follow.

The flow has three commands:
1. `helm package chart/hello-devops` makes `hello-devops-0.2.0.tgz`, named after the chart version.
2. `helm push hello-devops-0.2.0.tgz oci://ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/charts` uploads it to GitHub's registry, next to your image from Day 21.
3. `helm install hello oci://ghcr.io/<your-github-user>/charts/hello-devops --version 0.2.0` installs it on any cluster.

Log in once with `helm registry login ghcr.io -u <your-github-user>` and a GitHub token that can write packages. Always pin `--version`, for the same reason you never deploy `:latest` images: you want the same chart today and next month. Most third-party projects publish this way now. Envoy Gateway's chart on Day 36 came from `oci://docker.io/envoyproxy/gateway-helm`.

Your `Chart.yaml` holds two version numbers, and people mix them up. The `version` field is the chart's own version: bump it on every change to the chart, so one number always means the same files. The `appVersion` field is the version of the app inside, which the lab chart uses as the default image tag.

Kustomize is built into kubectl, and you have already used it: `kubectl apply -k k8s` reads `k8s/kustomization.yaml`. That folder is the base. An **overlay** is another folder with its own `kustomization.yaml` that points at the base and lists changes:
- `resources: [../../k8s]` pulls in the base. An overlay can add files too, such as prod's `pdb.yaml`.
- `namespace: hello-prod` moves every object into one namespace, and renames the Namespace object as well.
- `images` changes an image tag without touching the Deployment file.
- `replicas` sets a Deployment's replica count, and `labels` adds a label such as `env: prod` to every object and Pod.
- `patches` changes anything else.

Patches come in two styles. A strategic merge patch looks like a small piece of the object with only the changed fields; prod's `deployment-patch.yaml` is one. A JSON patch is a list of operations, such as "replace `/spec/minReplicas` with 4". JSON patches suit one exact field, or removing one, like the `nodePort` that both overlays drop.

Kustomize has a layout rule that trips people up. An overlay cannot live inside its base folder. An overlay at `k8s/overlays/prod` that points at `../../` fails with "cycle detected", because the base would contain the overlay. That is why the lab keeps `overlays/` next to `k8s/`.

Three commands do the work: `kubectl kustomize overlays/prod` prints the result, `kubectl diff -k overlays/prod` shows what would change in the cluster, and `kubectl apply -k overlays/prod` applies it.

Should we template or patch Kubernetes manifests? Helm vs Kustomize side by side

sections.body:
Pick the tool that matches the job:
- Someone else's software, such as Envoy Gateway, metrics-server or a monitoring stack: Helm. That is how those projects ship, and their values are the supported way to configure them.
- Your own app with a few differences per environment: either works. Kustomize keeps every file as plain YAML that anyone can read.
- Your own app installed by many teams with many settings: Helm, because values give each team one clear place to set things.

They also combine. You can render a chart with `helm template` and keep the output as a Kustomize base. Kustomize can also render charts itself through its `helmCharts` field, with the `--enable-helm` flag. Argo CD (Day 39) renders both straight from git, and Day 40 builds on these overlays to move a release from one environment to the next.

Each tool has a way to go wrong. Helm templates get hard to read once every field becomes a value; a `values.yaml` that repeats the whole Deployment has gone too far. Kustomize gets confusing when an overlay changes half the base; then the base is wrong, and should change instead.

My default for a team's own services is Kustomize with one base and small overlays, and Helm for everything installed from outside.

lessons.analogy: Helm is a recipe card with blanks: "___ grams of sugar, bake for ___ minutes". The `values.yaml` file holds the usual amounts, and your values file changes a few. The kitchen logbook, the release history, lets you bake an earlier version again. Kustomize is a master drawing with sheets of tracing paper on top: the drawing stays as it is, and each sheet adds the changes for one environment. Where it breaks: a recipe makes a new cake each time, while `helm upgrade` changes the cake that is already on the table.

code.title: overlays/dev/kustomization.yaml
code.src:
# The dev environment: the base in k8s/ plus a few changes (Day 37).
#   Preview: kubectl kustomize overlays/dev
#   Apply:   kubectl apply -k overlays/dev
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - ../../k8s # the base: every file listed in k8s/kustomization.yaml
namespace: hello-dev # move everything into its own namespace (the Namespace object is renamed too)
labels:
  - pairs:
      env: dev
    includeTemplates: true # also put the label on the Pods
images:
  - name: hello-devops
    newTag: "1.1.0" # dev runs the newest build
replicas:
  - name: hello-devops
    count: 1
patches:
  # Say which environment answers.
  - target:
      kind: ConfigMap
      name: hello-config
    patch: |-
      - op: replace
        path: /data/GREETING
        value: "Hello from dev!"
  # One or two Pods are enough in dev.
  - target:
      kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
      name: hello-devops
    patch: |-
      - op: replace
        path: /spec/minReplicas
        value: 1
      - op: replace
        path: /spec/maxReplicas
        value: 2
  # NodePort 30080 belongs to the base app in namespace hello, and two Services
  # cannot share one NodePort. Use a ClusterIP Service and port-forward instead.
  - target:
      kind: Service
      name: hello-devops
    patch: |-
      - op: replace
        path: /spec/type
        value: ClusterIP
      - op: remove
        path: /spec/ports/0/nodePort

#   Preview: kubectl kustomize overlays/prod
#   Apply:   kubectl apply -k overlays/prod
apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Kustomization
resources:
  - ../../k8s # the base
  - pdb.yaml # prod only: a PodDisruptionBudget
namespace: hello-prod
labels:
  - pairs:

    includeTemplates: true
images:
  - name: hello-devops
    newTag: "1.0.0" # prod runs the release that already passed dev
replicas:
  - name: hello-devops
    count: 4 # the same as minReplicas below, so kubectl apply and the HPA agree
patches:
  # More memory and a spread over nodes (a strategic merge patch in its own file).
  - path: deployment-patch.yaml
    target:
      kind: Deployment
      name: hello-devops
  # Say which environment answers.
  - target:
      kind: ConfigMap
      name: hello-config
    patch: |-
      - op: replace
        path: /data/GREETING
        value: "Hello from prod!"
  # Prod scales between 4 and 10 Pods.
  - target:
      kind: HorizontalPodAutoscaler
      name: hello-devops
    patch: |-
      - op: replace
        path: /spec/minReplicas
        value: 4
      - op: replace
        path: /spec/maxReplicas
        value: 10

  - target:
      kind: Service
      name: hello-devops

code.src:
# A strategic merge patch: write only the fields that change. Kustomize merges them
# into the Deployment named in kustomization.yaml (target), and matches containers by name.
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: hello-devops
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      affinity:
        podAntiAffinity:
          # Prefer to put hello-devops Pods on different nodes, so one node failure
          # does not take them all. "Preferred" means the scheduler may still
          # stack them if it has no other choice.
          preferredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
            - weight: 100
              podAffinityTerm:
                topologyKey: kubernetes.io/hostname
                labelSelector:
                  matchLabels:
                    app: hello-devops
      containers:
        - name: web
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: 200m
              memory: 192Mi
            limits:
              memory: 384Mi

lessons.mistake: You run `helm upgrade` with one new `--set`, and settings you gave at install time quietly disappear. When you pass any values on an upgrade, Helm starts from the chart's defaults plus only those values. Keep your settings in a values file such as `chart/kind-values.yaml`, pass it with `-f` on every install and upgrade, and check with `helm get values`.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences how Helm and Kustomize each turn one set of files into a dev and a prod version of an app. Say which you would use for hello-devops and why.
explain_back.answer: Helm keeps templates with blanks and fills them from a values file. Dev and prod are then two values files for the same chart, and each install is a release with revisions. Kustomize keeps plain YAML as a base and puts each environment's changes in an overlay folder, as patches, image tags and replica counts. Both produce ordinary YAML that the cluster applies. For hello-devops I would use Kustomize, because the differences are small and the files stay readable, and keep Helm for the third-party tools I install.

recap: Helm templates with values; Kustomize patches a plain base. Both render ordinary YAML.
A chart is Chart.yaml, values.yaml, templates, helpers and NOTES; render with `helm template` before installing.
Every install, upgrade and rollback is a revision; rollback adds a new one instead of rewriting history.
Passing values on upgrade drops earlier ones, so pass the same values file every time.
Helm 4: server-side apply for new releases, `--rollback-on-failure` and `--force-replace`; Helm 3 security fixes end February 10, 2027.
Overlays point at a base with `resources`, then set namespace, images, replicas, labels and patches; never put them inside the base.

check.q: A chart's `values.yaml` says `replicaCount: 2`. You installed with `-f prod.yaml`, which sets 5. Now you run `helm upgrade web ./chart --set image.tag=1.2.0` only. How many replicas run afterwards?
options: 5, because Helm keeps install values forever
6, because Helm adds the counts together
1, because `--set` resets every value to 1
2, because the upgrade starts from the chart defaults
check.why: Passing any values on upgrade means chart defaults plus only the new values, so prod.yaml's 5 is dropped and the default 2 applies.

check.q: Prod needs a bigger memory limit on the base Deployment's `web` container, and nothing else changes. What do you add to the prod overlay?
options: A strategic merge patch with only that container's resources
A full copy of deployment.yaml with the new limit
An `images` entry with a new tag
A `configMapGenerator` with a MEMORY key
check.why: A strategic merge patch names the Deployment and container and lists only the changed fields; Kustomize merges it into the base.

check.q: An old CI script runs `helm upgrade --install api ./chart --atomic`. What happens with Helm 4?
options: It fails, because Helm 4 removed the flag
It ignores the flag and never rolls back
It works, with a warning to use the new name
It switches the release to client-side apply
check.why: Helm 4 renamed `--atomic` to `--rollback-on-failure` and keeps the old name working with a deprecation warning.

interview.q: When would you choose Helm, and when Kustomize?
interview.a: Helm is a package manager with templates and release history, and it is the standard way to install and upgrade third-party software. Kustomize keeps plain YAML and adds per-environment overlays, which suits a team's own services with small differences. Helm's templates are powerful but get hard to read, while Kustomize gets messy if overlays rewrite most of the base. Many teams use Helm for platform tools and Kustomize for their own apps, and GitOps tools such as Argo CD render both.

interview.q: What is a Helm release, and how does a rollback work?
interview.a: A release is one installed copy of a chart, with a name, a namespace and a numbered history of revisions stored as Secrets. Each install, upgrade or rollback adds a revision. It holds the rendered manifest and the values used. `helm rollback` re-applies an earlier revision's manifest and records it as a new revision, so history is never lost. In Helm 4 it also keeps the apply method the release started with, client-side or server-side.

interview.q: How do you manage different settings for dev, staging and prod?
interview.a: I keep one source of truth for the app and express each environment as a small difference. With Helm that is one values file per environment; with Kustomize, one overlay per environment. Image tags are pinned per environment, so promotion is a reviewed change that copies a tag from one environment to the next. Secrets stay out of those files and come from a secret manager. Rendering every environment in CI, with `helm template` or `kubectl kustomize`, catches mistakes before they reach a cluster.

deeper.body:
Helm keeps its memory inside the cluster. Each revision of a release is a Secret of type `helm.sh/release.v1` in the release's namespace, named like `sh.helm.release.v1.hello.v3`. List them with `kubectl get secrets -n hello-helm -l owner=helm`. Each one holds the chart, the values and the rendered manifest, compressed and encoded. Helm keeps the last 10 revisions per release by default; `--history-max` changes that.

This design has a consequence: Helm only knows what it applied, not what is in the cluster now. If someone runs `kubectl edit` on a Deployment that Helm manages, Helm does not notice until the next upgrade. What happens then depends on the apply method:
- With server-side apply, the default for new Helm 4 releases, the API server tracks which manager owns each field. A field changed by hand now has a different owner, so Helm can report a conflict instead of silently overwriting it. `--force-conflicts` takes the field back.
- With client-side apply, Helm compares the old manifest, the new one and the live object, and patches the difference. Hand edits to fields the chart does not set survive; edits to fields it does set are overwritten.

Either way, hand edits make the next upgrade harder to predict. Argo CD (Day 39) fixes this by watching for drift all the time and showing it.

Two Helm features you will meet in third-party charts:
- Hooks: templates with a `helm.sh/hook` annotation run at set points, such as a database migration Job before an upgrade.
- Tests: Pods with the `test` hook that `helm test <release>` runs after an install, to check the app answers.

On the Kustomize side, look at `configMapGenerator`. It builds a ConfigMap from literals or files and adds a hash of the content to its name, such as `hello-config-h622489h5k`. Kustomize also updates every reference to that name. Change a value, the name changes, the Pod template changes, and the Deployment rolls out by itself. It is the Kustomize version of the chart's `checksum/config` trick.

lessons.title: Troubleshooting Kubernetes
lessons.goal: By the end you can find out why a workload is broken with a fixed order of kubectl commands, read the common failure states, test from inside Pods that have no tools, and tell an RBAC "forbidden" from a bug.

guess.q: A Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff, and `kubectl logs` on it shows nothing useful. Where is the error message most likely to be?
options: Nowhere: a crashing app never writes its error
Only in etcd, which kubectl cannot read
In the previous container's log: `kubectl logs --previous`
On the node's disk, which you must open with SSH
guess.why: After a restart, `kubectl logs` shows the new container, which may have printed nothing yet. `--previous` shows the container that crashed, error and all.

terms.plain: A short record that a Kubernetes part wrote about an object, such as a failed probe; kept about an hour.
A container keeps exiting, and Kubernetes waits longer before each restart, up to 5 minutes.
The node failed to get the image and now waits longer between tries.
The image is there, but the container's settings cannot be built, usually a missing ConfigMap or Secret.
A temporary extra container that kubectl debug adds to a running Pod for checks.
Role-based access control: rules that say who may do which actions on which objects.
A Role lists allowed actions in one namespace; a RoleBinding gives that Role to someone.
An identity for a program, such as a CI job or a Pod that calls the Kubernetes API.

sections.body:
When something breaks, the urge is to change three things and hope. Kubernetes punishes that. Many parts react on their own, so a guess can change the evidence before you have read it. A fixed order of checks is faster, even when you think you already know the answer.

Work from the bottom up, because each layer depends on the one below it:
1. The Pod: is it scheduled, running, ready, restarting?
2. The Service: does it select those Pods, and does its `targetPort` match the port the app listens on?
3. The route: does the Gateway or Ingress send traffic to that Service?
4. The node: if many Pods fail together, is one node short of memory or not ready?

For each layer, the commands are nearly always the same:
1. `kubectl get` for STATUS, READY and RESTARTS.
2. `kubectl describe`, reading the Events at the bottom first.
3. `kubectl logs`, with `--previous` if the container restarted.
4. `kubectl get events` for the whole namespace, sorted by time.
5. `kubectl exec`, `port-forward` or `debug` to test from inside.

Two habits help more than any tool. Change one thing at a time, then watch what happens. And test layers one by one: `kubectl port-forward pod/<pod>` skips the Service, so if the Pod answers there and not through the Service, you know which layer to read.

Troubleshooting Pods in CrashLoopBackOff, Pending and ImagePullBackOff

sections.body:
In these four states the container has not run yet, so `kubectl logs` has nothing to show. The answer is in `kubectl describe pod`, under Events:
- `Pending`: no node will take the Pod. Usual causes: requests larger than any node's free room, a PVC that cannot bind, or a nodeSelector, affinity or taint that rules out every node.
- `ContainerCreating` for more than a minute: the node is still setting the Pod up. Usually a volume that will not mount, or a large image still downloading.
- `ErrImagePull`, then `ImagePullBackOff`: the node cannot get the image. Check the name and tag, the registry login for private images, and on kind whether you ran `kind load docker-image`.
- `CreateContainerConfigError`: the image is there, but the kubelet cannot build the container's settings. Almost always a missing ConfigMap or Secret, or a missing key in one.

"BackOff" in a status only means the kubelet now waits longer between tries. It is never the cause. Look for the first error in the Events.

For `Pending`, the scheduler writes a `FailedScheduling` event, and it pays to read it slowly. A message that starts `0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s), 2 Insufficient cpu` counts all three nodes. One is ruled out by a taint (kind's control plane, Day 35), and two lack free CPU for the request. Lower the request, remove other workloads, or add a node.

Here the container ran at least once, so there is evidence in its logs and in its last state:
- `CrashLoopBackOff`: the container keeps exiting, and the kubelet waits longer before each restart: 10 seconds, then 20, 40, up to 5 minutes. It is a symptom. Read `kubectl logs --previous` for the app's own error, then `Last State` in describe.
- `OOMKilled`: `Last State` shows `Reason: OOMKilled` and `Exit Code: 137`. The container went over its memory limit (Day 35).
- Restarts with clean logs: often a liveness probe that fails. The Events say `Liveness probe failed` and then that the container will be restarted. The app was fine; the check was wrong.
- `Running` but `0/1` READY: the readiness probe fails, so the Pod gets no traffic. The Events show `Readiness probe failed` with a status code or an error.
- All Pods ready, but the Service still fails: the Service matches no Pods. `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>` shows `<unset>` under ENDPOINTS.

For that last case, compare the Service's selector (`kubectl describe service`) with the Pods' labels (`kubectl get pods --show-labels`), and check that `targetPort` is the port the app listens on. This one fools people, because every Pod looks healthy.

Remember that the STATUS column is a summary kubectl writes for you. `CrashLoopBackOff` is not a Pod phase; the phase is still `Running`. When the column confuses you, `kubectl get pod <name> -o yaml` shows the real fields under `status`.

Events are short records that Kubernetes parts write about objects: the scheduler placed a Pod, the kubelet pulled an image, a probe failed. The API server keeps them for about an hour by default, so read them early.

Three ways to read them:
- `kubectl describe pod <name>` shows one object's events at the bottom.
- `kubectl get events -n <ns> --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp` lists the namespace's events, oldest first.
- `kubectl events -n <ns> --for pod/<name>` is the newer command. It sorts by time on its own, and `--types=Warning` hides the routine ones.

Logs are what the container wrote to standard output and standard error. `kubectl logs <pod>` reads the current container. Right after a crash, that is a fresh container that may not have printed anything yet. `--previous` reads the one before, the one that crashed. Add `-c <container>` when a Pod has more than one container, and `-f` to follow new lines.

The exit code under `Last State` narrows things down fast:
- 0: the process finished on purpose. In a Deployment that still counts as a restart, because a web app should never finish.
- 1, or another small number: the app exited with its own error. Read the logs.
- 137: killed with SIGKILL (128 + 9). Most often the OOM killer, or an app that ignored the stop signal until its grace period ran out.
- 143: stopped with SIGTERM (128 + 15), the polite stop signal Kubernetes sends first.

sections.h: Looking inside: exec, port-forward and kubectl debug
sections.body:
Sometimes you need to test from inside the cluster. Can this Pod resolve a name, reach a port, see a file?

The command `kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh` opens a shell in a running container. That only works if the image has a shell and the tools you need. Small images often do not. The hello-devops image has `sh` and Python, but no `nslookup`, `curl` or `wget`. Distroless images have no shell at all.

That is what `kubectl debug` is for. It adds an **ephemeral container** to a running Pod: a temporary extra container with an image you choose, such as `busybox`, or `nicolaka/netshoot`, a large image full of network tools. It shares the Pod's network, so it sees DNS and ports exactly as the app does. With `--target=web` it also sees the processes of the `web` container. Ephemeral containers are never restarted, and they go away when the Pod is deleted. Two more forms:
- `kubectl debug <pod> -it --copy-to=<pod>-debug --container=web -- sh` makes a copy of the Pod with a shell, for a container that crashes too fast to inspect.
- `kubectl debug node/<node> -it --image=ubuntu` starts a Pod on that node with the node's files mounted at `/host`.

For DNS and network checks you often do not need the broken Pod at all. A throwaway Pod is enough: `kubectl run net-test -n hello --rm -it --image=busybox:1.37 --restart=Never -- nslookup redis.hello.svc.cluster.local`. NXDOMAIN means the name is wrong or the Service does not exist. If the name resolves but connections fail, check the Service's endpoints next.

sections.body:
Sooner or later you will see `Error from server (Forbidden)`. That is not a bug in your YAML. The API server understood the request and refused it, because the person or program behind it lacks permission.

Kubernetes decides with role-based access control (RBAC), and four kinds of object do the work:
- A Role lists allowed actions in one namespace, such as `get`, `list` and `watch` on `pods`. A ClusterRole does the same for the whole cluster.
- A RoleBinding gives a Role to subjects in one namespace. A ClusterRoleBinding gives a ClusterRole everywhere.
- Subjects are users, groups and ServiceAccounts. A ServiceAccount is an identity for a program, such as a CI job or a Pod that calls the API.

Permissions only add up. There are no deny rules, so "forbidden" always means that nothing allowed the action.

The error tells you exactly what was missing, for example: `User "system:serviceaccount:hello:viewer" cannot delete resource "pods" in API group "" in the namespace "hello"`. Read it as subject, verb, resource, API group and namespace. Then ask the cluster directly:
- `kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n hello` answers yes or no for you.
- Add `--as=system:serviceaccount:hello:viewer` to ask on behalf of someone else. Your kind admin user is allowed to do that.

Fix it with the smallest Role that does the job. Binding a robot to `cluster-admin` makes the error go away, and also opens the whole cluster to that robot. RBAC is also how you keep Secrets private (Day 34): very few Roles should allow `get` or `list` on `secrets`.

sections.h: Faster tools, and when the node is the problem
sections.body:
A few tools save time once the method is in your head:
- `kubectl top pods` and `kubectl top nodes` show live CPU and memory use, from the metrics-server you installed on Day 35. Check them before you raise a limit.
- k9s is a terminal UI over the same API. You move between Pods, logs, events and describe output with a few keys. Install it with `brew install derailed/k9s/k9s` and run `k9s -n debug-lab`.
- Headlamp is a graphical alternative. The old Kubernetes Dashboard project has been archived, and the [Kubernetes blog](https://kubernetes.io/blog/2026/06/01/dashboard-to-headlamp/) points to Headlamp instead.

Learn the plain kubectl commands first anyway. k9s is not installed on every machine you will log in to; kubectl is.

If many Pods fail at once, and all on one node, look at the node. The command `kubectl get nodes` shows `NotReady` when a kubelet stops reporting. Then `kubectl describe node <name>` shows conditions such as `MemoryPressure` and `DiskPressure`, and lists the Pods on the node with their requests. On kind, a node is a Docker container. Run `docker stats` on your Mac to see whether Docker Desktop itself is short of memory; its settings let you give it more.

steps.say: Set this up on purpose: change `REDIS_HOST` in the lab's ConfigMap to `rediss`, one letter too many, and restart the Deployment so new Pods read it. This is a typical real mistake.
steps.code:

$ kubectl rollout restart deployment/hello-devops -n hello

steps.say: The symptom: the rollout never finishes. One new Pod is Running but not ready. The three old Pods keep serving, because the Deployment uses `maxUnavailable: 0` and readiness gates the rollout. Users see nothing wrong yet.
steps.code:

code.title: k8s-broken/README.md
code.src:
# Break-and-fix lab (Day 38)

A small online shop runs five services. Each one is broken in a different way.
Your job: find out why with `kubectl`, fix the YAML file, apply it again, and check the fix.

Do not open `SOLUTIONS.md` until you have tried each one. The skill you are practising is the
search, not the answer.

## Before you start

- Your kind cluster from Day 30 is running (`kubectl get nodes` shows three Ready nodes).
- The image is loaded into the cluster: `kind load docker-image hello-devops:1.0.0 --name devops`.
- Optional: metrics-server from Day 35, so `kubectl top` works.

## Start the lab

```bash
kubectl apply -f k8s-broken/
kubectl get pods -n debug-lab -w
```

Wait about two minutes before you start. Some problems only show after a few restarts.

## What the shop team reports

| Service | File | What people see |
|---|---|---|
| catalog | `01-catalog.yaml` | The Pod never starts. Its STATUS is `ErrImagePull`, then `ImagePullBackOff`. |
| checkout | `02-checkout.yaml` | The Pod stays `0/1` with STATUS `CreateContainerConfigError`. `kubectl logs` shows nothing. |
| search | `03-search.yaml` | Both Pods are `Running` and `1/1` Ready, but requests to `http://search.debug-lab` fail. |
| reports | `04-reports.yaml` | RESTARTS keeps going up. STATUS switches between `OOMKilled` and `CrashLoopBackOff`. |
| profile | `05-profile.yaml` | The Pod is `Running` and Ready, then restarts every half a minute or so. The logs look normal. |

To test the search service from inside the cluster, start a throwaway Pod:

```bash
kubectl run net-test -n debug-lab --rm -it --image=busybox:1.37 --restart=Never -- wget -qO- -T 3 http://search
```

## The method (use it for every service)

1. `kubectl get pods -n debug-lab`: which Pod, which STATUS, how many RESTARTS.
2. `kubectl describe pod <pod> -n debug-lab`: read the Events at the bottom first, then `Last State`.
3. `kubectl logs <pod> -n debug-lab --previous`: what the crashed container printed before it died.
4. `kubectl get events -n debug-lab --sort-by=.metadata.creationTimestamp`: everything that happened, in order.
5. For a Service: `kubectl get endpointslices -n debug-lab -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<service>`.
6. Compare what you found with the YAML file. Change one thing, `kubectl apply -f` the file, and watch again.

## You are done when

- `kubectl get pods -n debug-lab` shows every Pod `Running`, `1/1` Ready, and RESTARTS no longer going up for two minutes.
- The `net-test` command above prints JSON from the search service.

Clean up with `kubectl delete namespace debug-lab`.

steps: Check that `hello-devops:1.0.0` is loaded into kind and metrics-server is running. Copy the `k8s-broken/` folder into your repo.

Fix one file at a time, apply it, and wait until that Pod is healthy before you move to the next.
Prove that search works with the `net-test` busybox command from the README.

RBAC: create a ServiceAccount `viewer` in `debug-lab`, a Role that may only get, list and watch Pods, and a RoleBinding. Check with `kubectl auth can-i` that it may list Pods but not delete them, then trigger the Forbidden error with `--as`.
Compare your notes with `SOLUTIONS.md` in the lab folder, then delete the `debug-lab` namespace.
hints: If `kubectl logs` shows nothing, ask whether the container ever started. If it never did, the answer is in the Events.
`kubectl get pod <pod> -n debug-lab -o jsonpath='{.status.containerStatuses[0].lastState}'` prints the last crash on one line.
For RBAC you need three commands: `kubectl create serviceaccount`, `kubectl create role` and `kubectl create rolebinding`. The commands list has the last two.
task.done_when: All five Pods in `debug-lab` are Running and 1/1 Ready with no new restarts, `net-test` gets JSON from search, and `kubectl auth can-i delete pods -n debug-lab --as=system:serviceaccount:debug-lab:viewer` says no.

explain_back.prompt: Explain in 3 to 4 sentences how you would find out why a Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. Mention which commands you run, in which order, and what each one can tell you.
explain_back.answer: First `kubectl get pods` to see the status and how many restarts there have been. Then `kubectl describe pod` and read the Events and `Last State`: the exit code tells me whether it was the app's own error, an OOM kill (137) or a failed liveness probe. Then `kubectl logs --previous`, because the current container may have printed nothing yet, while the crashed one has the error. If that is still not enough, I compare the config the Pod got, such as env vars, ConfigMaps and probes, with what the app expects.

recap: Debug bottom-up: Pod, then Service, then route, then node. Change one thing at a time.
Pending, ContainerCreating, ImagePullBackOff and CreateContainerConfigError: no logs yet, read the Events.
CrashLoopBackOff is a symptom; `logs --previous` and the exit code in Last State show the cause.
Healthy Pods but a failing Service usually means a selector or targetPort mismatch: check EndpointSlices.
`kubectl debug` adds an ephemeral container with tools; a throwaway busybox Pod checks DNS.
A Forbidden error comes from RBAC: read the message, ask `kubectl auth can-i`, grant the smallest Role.

check.q: A new Pod stays Pending. Its event says `0/3 nodes are available: 1 node(s) had untolerated taint(s), 2 Insufficient memory`. What is the most likely fix?
options: Raise the Pod's memory limit
Remove the taint from every node
Lower the memory request, or free up room
Add a readiness probe to the Pod
check.why: The two workers lack free memory for the request, and scheduling uses requests, so the request must shrink or room must appear.

check.q: A Pod shows `CreateContainerConfigError` and `kubectl logs` prints nothing. Why are the logs empty?
options: The container never started, so there is nothing to log; the Events explain why
The logs were deleted when the Pod restarted
The app writes logs to a file instead of standard output
kubectl needs `--previous` for every Pod with an error
check.why: The kubelet could not build the container's settings, usually because a ConfigMap or Secret is missing, so no process ever ran.

check.q: A CI job's ServiceAccount `deployer` in namespace `ci` gets Forbidden when it applies a Deployment to namespace `shop`. Which command checks the permission directly?
options: Read the Deployment's events in `shop`
Read the CI job's logs once more
Restart the CI runner and try again
Run `kubectl auth can-i` as that ServiceAccount
check.why: `kubectl auth can-i create deployments -n shop --as=system:serviceaccount:ci:deployer` asks the API server about that exact subject, action and namespace.

interview.q: A Pod is in CrashLoopBackOff. Walk me through how you debug it.
interview.a: I start with `kubectl get pods` for the restart count, then `kubectl describe pod` for the Events and the Last State with its exit code. Exit code 137 with OOMKilled points at memory, and a failed liveness probe shows up in the Events. A small code such as 1 means the app exited with its own error. Then `kubectl logs --previous` shows what the crashed container printed. If the image has no tools, I use `kubectl debug` with an ephemeral container to check config, DNS or files from inside the Pod.

interview.q: The Pods are healthy, but requests to the Service fail. What do you check?
interview.a: First the Service's endpoints with `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>`; empty endpoints mean the selector matches no ready Pods. Then I compare the selector with `kubectl get pods --show-labels`, and check that `targetPort` matches the container's port. Next I test from inside the cluster with a throwaway busybox Pod, using the Service's DNS name, to rule out DNS. If all of that works, I look at NetworkPolicies and then at the Gateway or Ingress route in front of the Service.

interview.q: What is RBAC in Kubernetes, and how do you debug a Forbidden error?
interview.a: RBAC is role-based access control: Roles and ClusterRoles list allowed verbs on resources, and bindings give them to users, groups or ServiceAccounts. Permissions only add up; there are no deny rules. The Forbidden message names the subject, verb, resource and namespace, and `kubectl auth can-i` with `--as` confirms it. Then I add the smallest Role and RoleBinding that allow exactly that action, rather than a broad ClusterRole.

deeper.body:
Five more failures you will meet sooner or later, each with its first check:
- `exec format error` in the logs, right at start: the image was built for another CPU. On an Apple Silicon Mac, an image built only for amd64 cannot run on arm64 kind nodes. Build multi-platform images (Part 3) or pick an image that has an arm64 variant.
- `Init:CrashLoopBackOff` or `Init:0/1` for a long time: an init container fails or waits. Its logs need `-c <init-container-name>`.
- `Terminating` that never ends: something holds the object, often a finalizer waiting for a controller that is gone. `kubectl get pod <name> -o jsonpath='{.metadata.finalizers}'` shows it. Do not force-delete before you know what the finalizer protects.
- `Evicted` or `ContainerStatusUnknown` Pods left behind: the node ran short of memory or disk and evicted them (Day 35). The Deployment already replaced them; read the eviction message, then delete the leftovers.
- `Unable to connect to the server` from kubectl itself: the cluster is down or you are on the wrong context. `kubectl config current-context` should say `kind-devops`, and `docker ps` should show the kind node containers.

When the problem looks like the network, check in order: the name, the endpoints, the port, and then policy. A NetworkPolicy (Day 33) that selects a Pod blocks all traffic its rules do not allow. If `nslookup` works and the endpoints are there but connections time out, look for a policy with `kubectl get networkpolicy -n <ns>`.

At work, two more habits help. Write each incident down: the symptom, the command that showed the cause, the fix. After a few months that file is your team's best runbook. And automate the boring part: the `kubectl events --types=Warning` view and a few saved k9s shortcuts often find the problem before anyone opens a dashboard.

Finally, know where Kubernetes' own logs live. On kind, `docker exec devops-control-plane crictl ps` lists the control plane containers, and `kind export logs` collects logs from every node into a folder for you to read or attach to a bug report.

recap: Kubernetes stores your desired state and runs control loops that keep the cluster matching it.
Every component talks only to the API server: etcd stores state, the scheduler places Pods, kubelets run them.
A Pod is one or more containers with one IP address; Deployments create, replace and roll out Pods through ReplicaSets.
Services give changing Pods a stable name and address, and NetworkPolicies decide who may connect.
ConfigMaps and Secrets keep settings out of the image; env vars need a restart, and base64 is not encryption.
Probes decide when to wait, restart or stop traffic; requests place Pods and drive the HPA, and memory over the limit means OOMKilled.
The Gateway API (GatewayClass, Gateway, HTTPRoute) replaces the frozen Ingress API; ingress-nginx was retired in March 2026.
PVCs ask for storage, StorageClasses create it, and StatefulSets give each replica a stable name and its own disk.
Helm packages an app as a chart with values and versioned releases; Kustomize builds each environment as an overlay on a plain base.
Debug bottom-up with get, describe, logs `--previous`, events and EndpointSlices; Forbidden means RBAC, checked with `kubectl auth can-i`.

flashcards.front: What does a Kubernetes controller do?
flashcards.back: It compares desired state with actual state, again and again, and acts to close the gap.

flashcards.front: Which component is the only one that talks to etcd?
flashcards.back: The API server.

flashcards.front: A Pod stays Pending with no node assigned. Which component should have acted?
flashcards.back: The scheduler.

flashcards.front: Label or annotation: which one do selectors use?
flashcards.back: Labels. Annotations are notes for people and tools.

flashcards.front: How do you declare a native sidecar container?
flashcards.back: As an init container with `restartPolicy: Always`.

flashcards.front: Which Deployment changes create a new revision?
flashcards.back: Only changes to the Pod template, `spec.template`. Scaling does not.

flashcards.front: In a NodePort Service, what are port, targetPort and nodePort?
flashcards.back: port is the Service's port, targetPort is the Pod's port, nodePort is opened on every node.

flashcards.front: What is the DNS name of Service `redis` in namespace `hello`?
flashcards.back: `redis.hello.svc.cluster.local` (or just `redis` from inside `hello`).

flashcards.front: You changed a ConfigMap that Pods read through envFrom. What else must you do?
flashcards.back: Restart the Pods, for example with `kubectl rollout restart deployment/NAME`.

flashcards.front: Does base64 protect a Secret?
flashcards.back: No. Anyone can decode it; encryption at rest and RBAC protect Secrets.

flashcards.front: What happens when a readiness probe fails? And a liveness probe?
flashcards.back: Readiness: the Pod leaves the Service's endpoints but keeps running. Liveness: the kubelet restarts the container.

flashcards.front: A container shows OOMKilled and exit code 137. What happened?
flashcards.back: It used more memory than its limit, so the kernel killed it with SIGKILL (128 + 9).

flashcards.front: What does a container at its CPU limit experience?
flashcards.back: Throttling: it keeps running, only slower. It is not killed.

flashcards.front: What two things does a CPU-based HPA need?
flashcards.back: metrics-server (with `--kubelet-insecure-tls` on kind) and CPU requests on the Pods.

flashcards.front: What does a PodDisruptionBudget protect against, and what not?
flashcards.back: It limits planned disruptions such as `kubectl drain`; it cannot stop a node crash.

flashcards.front: Name the three main Gateway API objects and who usually owns each.
flashcards.back: GatewayClass (platform team), Gateway (cluster operators), HTTPRoute (app teams).

flashcards.front: What does kind's `standard` StorageClass do when you delete a PVC?
flashcards.back: Its reclaim policy is Delete, so the PV and the data folder are deleted too.

flashcards.front: What does `helm rollback app 1` write into the history?
flashcards.back: A new revision with the content of revision 1, described as "Rollback to 1".

flashcards.front: Why can a Kustomize overlay not live inside its base folder?
flashcards.back: Kustomize refuses it as a cycle: the base would contain the overlay.

flashcards.front: A Pod is in CreateContainerConfigError and its logs are empty. Where do you look?
flashcards.back: In `kubectl describe pod` Events: usually a missing ConfigMap, Secret or key.

quiz.q: On Day 15, Docker Compose ran hello-devops and Redis on your laptop. Which job can Kubernetes do that Compose cannot?
options: Start several containers from one YAML file
Run the containers of a failed machine on another machine
Give containers DNS names on a shared network
Restart a container after it crashes
quiz.why: Compose knows one machine; Kubernetes controllers notice lost Pods and the scheduler places replacements on healthy nodes.

quiz.q: A Service's Pods are Running and Ready, but `kubectl get endpointslices` for it lists no addresses. What is the most likely cause?
options: kube-proxy is in iptables mode
The Service type is ClusterIP
CoreDNS has crashed
The selector does not match the Pod labels
quiz.why: EndpointSlices list ready Pods that match the selector, so ready Pods with no endpoints point to a label mismatch.

quiz.q: A setup step must finish before the app starts, and both need the same files. What fits best?
options: An init container and an emptyDir volume shared with the app
A second Deployment that starts a minute earlier
A sidecar that runs the setup step every few minutes
A readiness probe that runs the setup script
quiz.why: Init containers run to completion before app containers start, and an emptyDir volume lets them hand files to the app.

quiz.q: You roll out a new image, then run `kubectl rollout undo`. Which revision number does the restored version get?
options: Its old number, which moves to the top of the list
Revision 0, the special number for rollbacks
A new, higher number, because the undo is itself a rollout
No number, because rollbacks are not recorded
quiz.why: An undo copies the old template back as a new rollout, so the old revision reappears under the next number.

quiz.q: A teammate pushed a Secret manifest with base64 values to a shared repo. What should happen first?
options: Nothing, because base64 values are encrypted
Rotate the leaked values, then delete the file from the repo
Re-encode the values twice, so they are harder to read
Make the repo private, then carry on as before
quiz.why: Base64 is readable and git keeps history, so the values must be treated as public and rotated.

quiz.q: An HPA targets 70m CPU per Pod (70% of a 100m request). 4 Pods now average 105m. How many replicas will it ask for, if `maxReplicas` is 10?
You want 20% of requests to reach a new version of the checkout service, through the existing Gateway. Which object do you change?
options: The HTTPRoute: two backendRefs with weights 80 and 20
The GatewayClass: a second controller for the new version
The Gateway: a second listener on another port
The Deployment: replicas set to 20% of the old count
quiz.why: Traffic splitting is a routing rule, so it lives in the HTTPRoute as weighted backends.

quiz.q: Every Pod of a Service is Running and 1/1 Ready, but requests to the Service fail, and its EndpointSlice shows `<unset>`. What is the most likely cause?
options: The readiness probe fails on every Pod
The memory limit is too low for the app
The image tag does not exist in the registry
The Service selector does not match the labels
quiz.why: Ready Pods that are missing from the endpoints are not selected at all, which points at the selector (or the targetPort).

quiz.q: Your team installs Envoy Gateway and a monitoring stack, and also deploys its own small service to dev and prod. Which split fits best?
options: Kustomize for everything, including the third-party tools
Helm for the tools, Kustomize overlays for your service
Copies of every YAML file per environment
One Helm chart that bundles all three together
quiz.why: Third-party projects ship and support Helm charts, while overlays keep a team's own few differences as plain, readable YAML.

quiz.q: Helm stores every revision of a release in the cluster, so it can show history and roll back. Which part of Terraform plays the same role of remembering what was deployed?
options: The provider block
The `.terraform.lock.hcl` file
The state file
The variables file
quiz.why: Terraform's state records what it created, just as Helm's release Secrets record what each revision applied.
